modules.title: Foundations of distributed systems
modules.summary: Why we split work across machines, what breaks when we do (partial failure, no shared clock), and the first real distributed program you build: MapReduce.

lessons.title: Why distribute — and the 8 fallacies
lessons.objective: By the end you can name the three reasons to distribute a system, list the eight fallacies of distributed computing, and point to the fallacy behind a given outage story.
concept: There are three honest reasons to put a system on more than one machine. **Scalability**: one box has a ceiling on CPU, RAM, disk and network bandwidth. **Fault tolerance**: one box will eventually die, and you want to keep serving when it does. **Latency**: users in Sydney should not wait for a round trip to Virginia. Everything else gets harder: failures become partial, there is no shared clock, and there is no shared memory. A single modern server has 100+ cores and terabytes of RAM, so the first design question is always: does this actually need to be distributed?

In the 1990s, engineers at Sun (L. Peter Deutsch, later James Gosling) wrote down eight assumptions that newcomers make and that fail in production: **the network is reliable; latency is zero; bandwidth is infinite; the network is secure; topology doesn't change; there is one administrator; transport cost is zero; the network is homogeneous.** Each one holds on `localhost`, which is exactly why code that passes every test on a laptop falls over in a datacenter.

The latency fallacy is the one you will meet weekly. A loop that makes one RPC per item costs 0.05 ms per call on localhost, so 10,000 items take half a second. Inside one datacenter at 0.5 ms per round trip it takes 5 seconds; across regions at 80 ms it takes over 13 minutes. Same code, three different products. The fixes are always the same shape: batch requests, paginate, run calls in parallel, or move the computation next to the data.

Failure is the other half. If one machine is up 99.9% of the time, independently, the chance that all 1,000 machines in a cluster are up at once is `0.999 ** 1000`, about 37%. At scale something is always broken, so a distributed system has to keep working while some of its parts are failing. That single requirement drives every topic in this stage: timeouts, replication, quorums, consensus and graceful degradation.

items.detail: Packets drop, switches reboot, cables get cut: every call needs a timeout and a retry policy.

items.label: Latency is zero
items.detail: A chatty loop of 1,000 RPCs at 80 ms each is 80 seconds.

items.detail: Internal traffic gets sniffed or spoofed; use mTLS between services.

items.label: Topology doesn't change
items.detail: IPs move during autoscaling and failover; hard-coded addresses break.

items.label: One administrator
items.detail: Another team changes a firewall rule or a DNS TTL you depend on.

items.label: Transport cost is zero
items.detail: Serialization CPU and cross-AZ/egress fees show up on the bill.

items.label: Network is homogeneous
items.detail: Mixed MTUs, NICs, kernels and client versions behave differently.

example.explain: The same sequential loop of 10,000 calls costs 0.5 s, 5.0 s and 800.0 s depending only on round-trip time. Nothing in the code changed; only the distance between caller and callee did.

lessons.tryit: Pick one public postmortem (the list at github.com/danluu/post-mortems has hundreds). In 5–6 sentences, state which of the eight fallacies the system assumed, what the symptom was, and what fix the authors applied. Then find one place in code you have written where a loop makes a network call per item, and estimate its runtime at 0.5 ms and 80 ms round-trip times.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the eight fallacies of distributed computing?
options: The network is reliable
Latency is zero
Clocks are synchronized
Topology doesn't change
questions.explain: The eight fallacies are all about the network: reliability, latency, bandwidth, security, topology, administration, transport cost and homogeneity. Clock skew is a real distributed-systems problem (lesson 3), but it is not on Deutsch's list.

questions.prompt: Each of 1,000 machines is independently up 99.9% of the time. What does this print?
questions.explain: 0.999^1000 ≈ 0.3677, which rounds to 0.37. Even with three nines per machine, all 1,000 are up at the same moment only about a third of the time; the tempting intuition that 'each one is almost always up, so the cluster is too' ignores that the probabilities multiply.

questions.prompt: A dashboard calls the profile service once per widget, sequentially, for 40 widgets. It loaded in 60 ms when both services were in the same rack. After the profile service moved to another region (90 ms RTT) the page takes about 3.7 s. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the client timeout so fewer calls fail
Add a batch endpoint that returns all 40 profiles in one round trip
Add more replicas of the profile service
Switch the payload from JSON to protobuf
questions.explain: 40 × 90 ms = 3.6 s is pure round-trip time (the latency-is-zero fallacy). One batched call costs one RTT. More replicas reduce load, not distance; protobuf shrinks bytes but the bottleneck is the number of round trips, not their size; raising the timeout changes nothing because calls are not failing.

questions.prompt: A cluster has 1,000 servers. Each server's mean time between failures is about 3 years (≈1,000 days). Roughly how often does some server in the cluster fail?
options: About once every 3 years
About once a month
About once a day
About once a minute
questions.explain: 1,000 servers ÷ 1,000 days per failure ≈ 1 failure per day. 'Every 3 years' is the per-machine rate; the cluster sees 1,000 times as many failures, so failure handling must be automatic, not a pager event.

video.title: The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing (Stephen Asbury)

lessons.why: Distribution buys scale and resilience at the cost of new failure modes. Knowing the fallacies lets you predict outages before they happen.

terms.d: Handling more load than one machine can.
Continuing to work when some machines fail.
Assumptions that fail in production, starting with 'the network is reliable' and 'latency is zero'.
Many small remote calls where one batched call would do.

mistakes.wrong: A remote call is just a slower function call.
mistakes.right: It can fail, time out or succeed without you knowing. Design every call for those outcomes.

mistakes.wrong: With reliable machines, failures are rare enough to ignore.
mistakes.right: At 1,000 machines at 99.9% each, all being up at once is under 37% likely. Failure is constant.

takeaways: Distribute for scalability, fault tolerance or latency, not by default.
Batch remote calls; one round trip per item adds up fast.
At scale, something is always failing.

lessons.title: Partial failure and timeouts
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain why a timeout cannot distinguish a dead node from a slow one, and choose a timeout and a retry policy (exponential backoff, jitter, retry budget) for a real RPC.
concept: On one machine, failure is mostly all-or-nothing: the process runs or it crashed. In a distributed system failure is **partial**: you send a request and hear nothing back. Maybe the request was lost, the server crashed before running it, the server ran it and crashed before replying, the reply was lost, or the server is alive but stuck in a 2-second GC pause. From the caller's side these cases are **indistinguishable**. The only tool is a timeout, and a timeout means 'I did not hear back in time', never 'it did not happen'.

Packet networks have **unbounded delay**: switches queue packets, TCP retransmits, receivers fall behind. So no timeout is 'correct'. Too short and you declare healthy-but-slow nodes dead, retry, and add load exactly when the system is struggling. Too long and users wait while threads and connections stay tied up. A practical rule is to measure the downstream's latency distribution and set the timeout just above a high percentile such as p99.9, then use a monotonic clock to measure it.

Retries turn a timeout into a recovery, but only for operations that are safe to repeat (next lesson). Use **exponential backoff** (`min(cap, base * 2**attempt)`) with **jitter** (pick a random delay up to that ceiling) so ten thousand clients that failed together don't retry together. Cap the total with a **retry budget**, for example retries may be at most 10% of requests. Retries multiply across layers: if each of three layers above a dead service makes 3 attempts, one user request becomes 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls to the dead service.

visual.title: Six different failures that all look like silence

items.label: Request lost
items.detail: Dropped by a switch; server never saw it. Retry is safe.

items.label: Server crashed before running it
items.detail: No effect happened. Retry is safe.

items.label: Server ran it, then crashed
items.detail: Effect happened, no reply. Retry duplicates it unless idempotent.

items.label: Reply lost
items.detail: Effect happened. Same danger as above.

items.label: Server is slow
items.detail: GC pause or overload; the reply may still arrive after you gave up.

items.label: Your own network is broken
items.detail: Every peer looks dead from here, but they are fine.

example.code:
import random

def backoff_delays(base=0.1, cap=5.0, attempts=6, seed=42):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    delays = []
    for i in range(attempts):
        ceiling = min(cap, base * 2 ** i)          # exponential, capped
        delays.append(round(rng.uniform(0, ceiling), 3))  # full jitter
    return delays

print(backoff_delays())
example.explain: Each attempt's ceiling doubles (0.1, 0.2, 0.4 … capped at 5 s) and the actual sleep is a uniform random value below it ('full jitter', as described in the AWS Builders' Library). Randomness spreads synchronized clients out so their retries do not arrive as one wave.

lessons.tryit: Write `call_with_retry(fn, attempts, base, cap)` that retries on `TimeoutError` using full-jitter backoff, plus a fake `fn` that raises `TimeoutError` 70% of the time. Run 1,000 simulated calls and print the success rate and total time slept. Then wrap it in three layers (each layer calls the one below through `call_with_retry` with 3 attempts) and count how many times the bottom `fn` runs when it always fails.

questions.prompt: A client sends an RPC and its timeout fires before any reply arrives. What can the client conclude?
options: The server crashed
The request was lost in the network
Nothing certain: the request may or may not have been executed
The server is overloaded and should be removed from the pool
questions.explain: A timeout only tells you that no reply arrived in time. The request could have been lost, executed with the reply lost, or still be running on a slow server. Each of the other options picks one cause out of several indistinguishable ones.

questions.prompt: What does this print (the backoff ceilings before jitter)?
questions.code:
base, cap = 0.1, 2.0
print([min(cap, base * 2 ** i) for i in range(6)])
questions.explain: The ceiling doubles each attempt: 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.6, then 3.2 is capped to 2.0. Multiplying by powers of two is exact in floating point, so no 0.30000000000000004-style noise appears. A common slip is forgetting the cap and writing 3.2 for the last value.

questions.prompt: A database has a 2-second GC pause. 10,000 clients call it with a 500 ms timeout and retry immediately, forever. Which change most directly prevents this pause from becoming a sustained outage?
options: Raise the timeout to 30 s
Exponential backoff with jitter plus a retry budget
Add another layer of retries at the load balancer
Lower the timeout to 100 ms so failures are detected faster
questions.explain: During the pause every client retries roughly four times, so the database wakes up to several times its normal load and may never catch up (a retry storm). Backoff with jitter spreads retries out and a budget caps the extra load. A 30 s timeout ties up client resources for every slow call; more retry layers multiply load; a shorter timeout creates even more retries.

questions.prompt: Services call each other in a chain A → B → C → D. Each of A, B and C makes up to 3 attempts (1 try + 2 retries) when its downstream call fails. D is completely down. How many requests reach D for one user request to A?
questions.explain: A tries B 3 times; each B attempt tries C 3 times (9 calls to C); each of those tries D 3 times: 3³ = 27. Picking 9 counts only two layers. This multiplication is why retries belong at one layer only, usually the outermost, or are governed by a shared budget.

lessons.why: Timeouts and retries are on every remote call you'll write. Getting them wrong turns a small slowdown into a retry storm that takes the whole system down.

terms.d: Some parts work while others don't, and you can't always tell which.
Giving up waiting; it can't distinguish dead from slow.
Wait `random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt))` before retrying.
A cap on retries, such as 10% of requests, to stop amplification.

mistakes.wrong: A timeout tells me the server didn't do the work.
mistakes.right: The request may have succeeded and only the reply was lost. Retries need idempotency.

mistakes.wrong: Retrying immediately and often is the most reliable approach.
mistakes.right: Synchronised retries pile onto a struggling service. Back off, add jitter and cap retries.

takeaways: No timeout is 'correct'; choose one from observed latency, like a bit above p99.
Back off exponentially with jitter.
Retry only idempotent operations, within a budget.

lessons.title: Clocks: physical, Lamport, vector
lessons.objective: By the end you can assign Lamport and vector timestamps to events in a message diagram and decide whether two events are causally ordered or concurrent.
concept: Every machine has a quartz clock that drifts, typically by tens of parts per million: 20 ppm is about 1.7 seconds per day. NTP corrects it, usually to within milliseconds on a good network, but a correction can make the time-of-day clock jump **backwards**. So use two different clocks: the time-of-day clock (`time.time()`) for timestamps humans read, and a **monotonic** clock (`time.monotonic()`) for measuring durations such as timeouts. Ordering writes by wall-clock timestamps (last-write-wins) silently drops data when clocks are skewed.

Lamport (1978) defined **happens-before** (→): a → b if a and b are on the same process and a comes first, or a is the send and b the receive of one message, or by transitivity. A **Lamport clock** is one counter per process: increment it before every event, attach it to every message, and on receive set `C = max(C, msg_ts) + 1`. The guarantee: if a → b then L(a) < L(b). The converse is false: L(a) < L(b) does not mean a caused b. Breaking ties by process id gives a total order consistent with causality.

A **vector clock** keeps one counter per process. On a local event or send, increment your own entry; on receive, take the element-wise max with the incoming vector, then increment your own entry. Now you can compare: if V(a) ≤ V(b) in every entry and they differ, then a → b; if neither is ≤ the other, a and b are **concurrent**. Dynamo-style stores use this (as version vectors) to detect conflicting writes and keep both versions as siblings instead of silently losing one. The cost is O(N) metadata per message.

Physical time can still be used safely if you know your error bound. Google Spanner's TrueTime API returns an interval [earliest, latest] guaranteed to contain the real time, and a transaction waits out that uncertainty (commit wait, a few milliseconds with GPS and atomic clocks) before its commit becomes visible. Hybrid logical clocks (HLC) combine a physical timestamp with a Lamport-style counter to get timestamps close to wall time that still respect causality.

visual.title: Lamport clocks: A sends to B, B replies
visual.code:
a = 0                 # process A's clock
b = 0                 # process B's clock
a = a + 1             # A: send event
msg = a               # message carries A's timestamp
b = max(b, msg) + 1   # B: receive
b = b + 1             # B: send reply
reply = b
a = max(a, reply) + 1 # A: receive reply
print(a, b)

example.explain: Vector clocks are compared entry by entry. [2,1,0] ≤ [2,2,0] everywhere, so the first event happened before the second. [2,0,0] is bigger in entry 0 and smaller in entries 1 and 2, so neither saw the other: they are concurrent.

lessons.tryit: On paper, draw three processes and six messages crossing between them. Label every event with its Lamport timestamp and its vector timestamp. Find a pair of events where L(a) < L(b) but the vectors show they are concurrent. Then implement a `VectorClock` class with `tick()`, `send()` and `receive(v)` and assert that it reproduces your hand-computed vectors.

questions.prompt: What does a Lamport clock guarantee for two events a and b?
options: If L(a) < L(b) then a happened before b
If a happened before b then L(a) < L(b)
Both directions: a → b exactly when L(a) < L(b)
L(a) equals the wall-clock time of a
questions.explain: Lamport clocks are consistent with causality in one direction only: a → b implies L(a) < L(b). Two concurrent events can still have L(a) < L(b), so you cannot read causality back out of the numbers; that is what vector clocks add.

questions.prompt: A process with Lamport clock 5 receives a message stamped 9, then performs one local event. What does this print?
questions.code:
c = 5
msg_ts = 9
c = max(c, msg_ts) + 1   # receive
c += 1                   # local event
print(c)
questions.explain: On receive, c = max(5, 9) + 1 = 10; the local event makes it 11. A common mistake is adding 1 to the local clock (6) instead of taking the max first, which would let the receive look 'earlier' than the send.

questions.prompt: Process 0 holds vector [3, 0, 1] and receives a message carrying [1, 4, 1]. What does this print?
questions.code:
mine = [3, 0, 1]
received = [1, 4, 1]
me = 0
mine = [max(x, y) for x, y in zip(mine, received)]
mine[me] += 1
print(mine)
questions.explain: Element-wise max gives [3, 4, 1]; then process 0 increments its own entry to get [4, 4, 1]. Incrementing before merging gives the same here, but the tempting error is to increment the sender's entry or every entry.

questions.prompt: Two datacenters replicate a key with last-write-wins using wall-clock timestamps. DC2's clock runs 300 ms behind. A user writes x=1 in DC1, then 100 ms later (real time) writes x=2 in DC2. After replication, what is x everywhere?
options: x=2, because it was written later
x=1: the newer write gets an older timestamp and is silently discarded
Both values are kept as siblings for the app to merge
Replication halts with a clock-skew error
questions.explain: DC2 stamps the second write with (t + 100 ms − 300 ms) = t − 200 ms, which is older than DC1's t, so LWW keeps x=1 and drops the user's latest write without any error. LWW never keeps siblings (that requires version vectors), and no store halts on skew it cannot see.

lessons.why: Ordering events across machines is impossible with wall clocks alone. Logical clocks let you say which event could have caused which.

terms.d: Quartz clocks gain or lose time; 20 ppm is about 1.7 seconds a day.
a → b if they're in order on one process, or a sends a message b receives, or transitively.
A counter that respects happens-before but can't detect concurrency.
One counter per process; compares events as before, after or concurrent.

mistakes.wrong: Timestamps from different machines tell me which event happened first.
mistakes.right: Clocks drift and can jump backwards. Use logical clocks for ordering.

mistakes.wrong: If L(a) < L(b) for Lamport clocks, a happened before b.
mistakes.right: The converse isn't guaranteed; concurrent events can have either order. Vector clocks can tell.

takeaways: Use monotonic clocks for durations, never wall clocks.
Lamport clocks give a consistent total order; vector clocks detect concurrency.
Physical time works only with a known error bound, as in Spanner's TrueTime.

lessons.title: RPC and idempotency
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain at-most-once, at-least-once and effectively-once semantics, and make a non-idempotent RPC safe to retry with an idempotency key.
concept: **RPC** (gRPC, Thrift, Go's `net/rpc` used in the 6.5840 labs) makes a remote call look like a local function call. The resemblance is dangerous. A local call returns or the whole process dies; a remote call can time out with an unknown outcome. A local call takes nanoseconds; a remote one takes 10⁵ times longer and varies wildly. Arguments must be serialized, so pointers and shared memory do not cross. Treat every RPC as sending a message and maybe getting one back.

Delivery semantics: **at-most-once** means send once and never retry, so the operation may be lost. **At-least-once** means retry until acknowledged, so the operation may run twice. True **exactly-once delivery** is impossible over a lossy network, but **effectively-once** processing is achievable: at-least-once delivery plus a receiver that makes duplicates harmless. Kafka, Stripe and the 6.5840 key/value lab all use this combination.

An operation is **idempotent** if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. `SET x = 5` and `DELETE /orders/42` are; `x += 5`, 'append to log' and 'charge $10' are not. To make a non-idempotent operation retry-safe, the client generates a unique **idempotency key** per logical operation and sends the same key on every retry. The server stores key → result atomically with the effect, and when it sees a key again it returns the stored result instead of redoing the work. In 6.5840 Lab 4 the key is (clientId, sequence number).

Three traps. First, the dedupe record must commit in the **same transaction** as the effect; if they are written separately, a crash between them recreates the duplicate. Second, keys need an expiry (Stripe keeps them about 24 hours), or the table grows forever. Third, two copies of the same request can arrive at the same time, so the check-and-insert needs a lock or a unique constraint, not a read followed by a write.

steps.label: Client creates key
steps.detail: UUID per logical operation, reused on every retry

steps.label: Send request + key
steps.detail: Idempotency-Key header or (clientId, seq) field

steps.label: Server looks up key
steps.detail: Seen before? Return the stored response

steps.label: Apply effect + store key
steps.detail: One transaction, so a crash leaves both or neither

steps.label: Reply (may be lost)
steps.detail: Client times out and retries with the same key; the duplicate is answered from the table

example.code:
import uuid

class PaymentServer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.balance = 100
        self.seen = {}                      # idempotency key -> response

    def charge(self, key, amount):
        if key in self.seen:
            return self.seen[key]           # duplicate: replay the old answer
        self.balance -= amount              # the effect ...
        self.seen[key] = ("ok", self.balance)  # ... and the record (one txn in real life)
        return self.seen[key]

s = PaymentServer()
k = str(uuid.uuid4())
print(s.charge(k, 30))   # first attempt      -> ('ok', 70)
print(s.charge(k, 30))   # retry after timeout -> ('ok', 70), not ('ok', 40)
example.explain: The retry carries the same key, so the server returns the stored response instead of charging again. In production, the balance update and the key insert must be in one database transaction.

lessons.tryit: Build a tiny HTTP or socket server with a `POST /transfer` endpoint and a client that randomly drops 30% of replies and retries. First run it without idempotency keys and count duplicate transfers over 1,000 requests. Then add keys stored in SQLite in the same transaction as the transfer, and show the duplicate count drops to zero, even if you kill the server mid-run.

questions.prompt: Which operation is idempotent?
options: DELETE /orders/42
POST /orders (create a new order)
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 10 WHERE id = 7
Append the line 'paid' to a log file
questions.explain: Deleting order 42 twice leaves the same state as deleting it once (the second call may return 404, but the data is the same). Creating, decrementing and appending each change state again on every repeat.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
seen = {}
balance = 100

def charge(key, amt):
    global balance
    if key in seen:
        return seen[key]
    balance -= amt
    seen[key] = balance
    return balance

charge("a1", 30)
charge("a1", 30)   # retry of the same logical charge
charge("b7", 30)   # a different charge
print(balance)
questions.explain: The first a1 charge takes 100 → 70, the retry of a1 is answered from `seen` without charging, and b7 is a new key so it takes 70 → 40. Answering 10 ignores the dedupe; answering 70 treats b7 as a duplicate even though its key differs.

questions.prompt: A payments service applies a charge in Postgres, then records the idempotency key in a separate Redis cache. It crashes after the Postgres commit but before the Redis write, and the client retries with the same key. What happens, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing bad: the retry finds the key in Redis
The customer is charged twice; store the key in the same Postgres transaction as the charge
The retry fails with an error, which is correct behaviour
The customer is charged twice; fix it by writing to Redis before Postgres
questions.explain: The key never reached Redis, so the retry looks new and charges again. Writing the key in the same transaction makes 'charged' and 'key recorded' commit together. Writing Redis first just moves the crash window: a crash after Redis but before Postgres makes the retry return 'ok' for a charge that never happened.

questions.prompt: In 6.5840 Lab 4, each Clerk tags requests with (clientId, seq) and the server remembers only the latest seq and reply per client. Why is storing only the latest one enough?
options: Because Go maps cannot hold more than one entry per key
Because a Clerk sends one request at a time and moves to seq+1 only after seq succeeds, so any request with seq ≤ latest is a duplicate
Because Raft already removes duplicate log entries
Because duplicates can only arrive within one second
questions.explain: The Clerk is sequential: it never sends seq+1 until seq has been answered. So the server only ever needs to answer the latest seq again; anything older is a stale duplicate whose reply the Clerk no longer waits for. Raft does not deduplicate: a retried command is a new log entry, which is exactly why the server needs the table.

mistakes.wrong: Exactly-once delivery is possible with the right protocol.

lessons.title: MapReduce
lessons.objective: By the end you can trace a word-count job through map, partition, shuffle and reduce, and explain how a MapReduce coordinator handles failed and slow workers.
concept: MapReduce (Dean & Ghemawat, OSDI 2004) lets you write two functions and run them on thousands of machines: `map(key, value) → list of (k2, v2)` and `reduce(k2, list of v2) → output`. The framework splits the input into M pieces, runs M map tasks, partitions each mapper's output into R buckets with `hash(k2) % R`, has each of the R reducers pull its bucket from every mapper (the **shuffle**), sorts by key, and calls reduce once per key. For word count, map emits `(word, 1)` and reduce sums the ones.

Fault tolerance is re-execution. The coordinator tracks every task as idle, in progress or completed. If a worker does not finish a task in time (the 6.5840 lab uses ten seconds), the task goes back to idle and another worker gets it. Completed **map** tasks on a dead worker are re-run too, because their output lived on that worker's local disk. Completed **reduce** output lives in the global file system, so it survives. This only works because map and reduce are deterministic.

Duplicates are normal: a 'dead' worker may only have been slow and finish later. Workers therefore write to a temporary file and **atomically rename** it (`os.Rename` in Go), so a reader never sees a half-written file and the last complete copy wins. Near the end of a job, the coordinator launches **backup** copies of the remaining in-progress tasks and takes whichever finishes first, because one machine with a bad disk can hold up the whole job. The paper reports that sort took 44% longer with backups disabled.

MapReduce also scheduled map tasks on machines that already held their input block, because in 2004 network bandwidth was the scarce resource. Its limits shaped what came next: it is batch-only, and every stage writes to disk, so iterative jobs such as PageRank, which chain many MapReduce rounds, are slow. Spark keeps intermediate data in memory and recovers lost partitions by recomputing them from their lineage.

Then simulate a crash: make the map 'worker' for document 2 raise an exception halfway, write coordinator logic that re-runs the failed task, and assert the final output is identical to a run with no crash.

questions.prompt: Why must a completed map task be re-executed when its worker dies, while a completed reduce task need not be?
options: Map tasks are cheaper, so re-running them is free
Map output is stored on the worker's local disk; reduce output is in the global file system
Reduce tasks are idempotent and map tasks are not
The coordinator only keeps a record of reduce tasks
questions.explain: Intermediate map output lives on the mapper's local disk, so it disappears with the machine, and reducers still need it. Reduce output is written to the shared file system and survives. Both functions must be deterministic; idempotency is not what distinguishes them.

questions.prompt: What does this word count print?

from collections import Counter

docs = ["a b a", "b c", "a"]
pairs = [(w, 1) for d in docs for w in d.split()]   # map
counts = Counter()
for w, one in pairs:                                  # reduce
    counts[w] += one
print(sorted(counts.items()))
questions.explain: The map emits a,b,a,b,c,a; the reduce sums per word, giving a=3, b=2, c=1, and `sorted` orders the pairs by word. Forgetting that 'a' appears twice in the first document gives a=2.

questions.prompt: The coordinator decides a map task is slow and gives it to a second worker. Both workers eventually finish and both write intermediate files for that task. What makes this safe?
options: The second worker detects the first and kills it
Each worker writes to a temp file and atomically renames it, map is deterministic, and the coordinator records only one completion
Reducers merge both copies and divide counts by two
It is not safe; the lab forbids reassigning tasks
questions.explain: Because map is deterministic, both copies contain the same data, and atomic rename means readers see one complete file, never a mix. Workers cannot reliably kill each other across a network, and dividing by two would break the moment only one copy finished.

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines into a reduce task that reads every mapper's bucket for reducer r, sorts, and writes its output atomically.
questions.explain: The list must exist before the loop fills it from all n_map files (mr-0-r, mr-1-r …). Sorting has to wait until every bucket has been read, so that all values for a key end up adjacent; grouping and writing come last, through a temp file plus rename.

mistakes.right: It may just be slow and finish later. Write to a temp file and atomically rename to make duplicates harmless.

mistakes.wrong: Map and reduce functions can have side effects.

project.title: MapReduce (MIT 6.5840 Lab 1)
project.brief: Implement the coordinator and worker for a distributed MapReduce in Go inside the 6.5840 lab skeleton, so the word-count, indexer, parallelism, early-exit and crash tests all pass. It exercises everything in this module: RPC between processes, timeouts to detect dead workers, re-execution of idempotent tasks, and atomic output.
milestones: Clone the 6.5840 repo, build the wc plugin and run mrsequential.go to produce the reference output; read the whole Lab 1 page and the MapReduce paper sections 3.1–3.3.

Define the RPCs in mr/rpc.go: a worker asks for a task; the coordinator replies with a map task (file name, task number, nReduce); the worker writes intermediate files mr-X-Y as JSON, bucketed by ihash(key) % nReduce.
Add the reduce phase: hand out reduce tasks only after every map task is complete; each reducer reads mr-*-Y, sorts by key, and writes mr-out-Y through a temp file plus os.Rename.

Add fault tolerance: reassign any task not reported complete within 10 seconds, ignore late completions of reassigned tasks, and make Done() return true only when every reduce task is finished; pass the crash and early-exit tests.
Run `make mr` (which runs the tests with -race) 20 times in a loop; fix every data race and every flaky failure until all runs pass.
project.stretch: Add backup tasks for stragglers: when no idle tasks remain, re-issue the oldest in-progress task. Add an artificial 5 s sleep to one worker's map function and measure total job time with and without backups.

exam.prompt: A 6.5840 worker is in a long GC pause while running a map task. The coordinator times it out after 10 s and gives the task to another worker. Then the first worker wakes up and finishes too. Why is the job's output still correct?
options: The coordinator kills the first worker over RPC
Map is deterministic and output is published by atomic rename, so both copies are identical and readers never see a partial file
The first worker notices the time jump and discards its output
Go's garbage collector never pauses longer than 10 s
exam.explain: The coordinator cannot tell slow from dead (partial failure), so the design must tolerate duplicate execution. Determinism makes the duplicates identical, and rename makes publication atomic. The coordinator has no way to reach or kill a paused process, and nothing makes the worker aware that it was declared dead.

exam.prompt: Using vector-clock comparison, what does this print?
exam.explain: [1,2,0] is smaller in entry 0 but larger in entry 1, so neither vector dominates: the events are concurrent. Summing the entries (3 vs 3) or comparing only the first entry are tempting shortcuts that lose exactly this information.

exam.prompt: A mobile app retries 'place order' with exponential backoff whenever a request times out. Which server design gives effectively-once order placement?
options: Retry with backoff alone is enough
Retries with the same client-generated order key, and the server inserts the order and the key in one transaction with a unique constraint on the key
Disable retries so each order is sent at most once
Have the server check a cache for recent identical orders by the same user
exam.explain: At-least-once delivery (retries) plus atomic dedupe on a stable key gives effectively-once. Backoff alone still duplicates; disabling retries loses orders; 'identical order by the same user' wrongly merges two real orders for the same item and is racy without a constraint.

exam.prompt: Process P's Lamport clock is 4. It receives a message stamped 2. What is P's clock after the receive event?
exam.explain: C = max(4, 2) + 1 = 5. The receive is a new event, so the clock must strictly increase even when the message is 'older'; answering 4 forgets the increment, and 3 uses the message's timestamp instead of the max.

exam.prompt: A downstream service's latency is p50 = 20 ms, p99 = 180 ms, p99.9 = 900 ms. You want fewer than 0.1% of calls to a healthy instance to be treated as failures, without holding threads longer than necessary. Which timeout fits?
options: 25 ms
200 ms
About 1 s
exam.explain: A timeout just above p99.9 (900 ms) misfires on under 0.1% of healthy calls. 200 ms misfires on about 1% of them and 25 ms on nearly half, each one triggering a retry; 30 s meets the goal but holds a thread 30× longer than needed whenever the instance really is dead.

exam.prompt: TCP already retransmits lost packets and delivers bytes in order. Why does an RPC service on top of TCP still need idempotency keys?
options: Because TCP only works inside one datacenter
Because TCP's guarantees end with the connection: if it breaks after the server acted but before the reply arrives, the client retries on a new connection that TCP cannot relate to the old one
Because TCP checksums are too weak to detect duplicates
It doesn't: TCP guarantees exactly-once delivery of RPCs
exam.explain: TCP deduplicates segments within one connection only. A reset, a crashed process or a failover to another server ends that connection, and the application's retry is new data on a new connection. Exactly-once semantics have to be built at the application layer, where the operation's identity is known.

exam.prompt: What is the worst-case total backoff (sum of the capped ceilings, no jitter) for 5 retries?
exam.code:
base, cap = 0.5, 4
print(sum(min(cap, base * 2 ** i) for i in range(5)))
exam.explain: The ceilings are 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and then 8 capped to 4, so the sum is 11.5 seconds. Without the cap the last term would be 8 and the total 15.5, which is why caps matter for user-facing timeouts.

modules.title: Storage engines & data
modules.summary: How databases lay bytes on disk, survive crashes, evolve their formats, copy data across machines and split it into shards — the parts you will implement in an LSM key/value store.

lessons.title: B-trees vs LSM trees
lessons.objective: By the end you can trace a read and a write through a B-tree and an LSM tree, and choose between them for a workload using write, read and space amplification.
concept: Almost every storage engine is one of two families. **B-trees** (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, SQLite) keep data in fixed-size pages (typically 4–16 KB) arranged as a balanced tree with a high branching factor. With 500 children per page and 4 KB pages, four levels address 500⁴ × 4 KB ≈ 256 TB, and the top levels stay in memory, so a point lookup costs about one disk read. Updates overwrite pages in place, and range scans walk the leaves in key order.

**LSM trees** (log-structured merge trees: RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra) never update in place. A write is appended to a log and inserted into an in-memory sorted **memtable**. When the memtable reaches a size limit (64 MB is a common default) it is flushed to disk as an immutable, sorted **SSTable**. A read checks the memtable, then SSTables from newest to oldest; a per-file **Bloom filter** skips files that cannot contain the key. Deletes write a **tombstone** marker, and background **compaction** merges files, dropping overwritten values and expired tombstones.

Compare them with three amplification numbers. **Write amplification** is bytes written to disk per byte the application wrote: a B-tree rewrites a whole page for a 100-byte change, while an LSM tree writes sequentially but rewrites each value at every compaction level (often 10–30× for leveled compaction). **Read amplification** is how many places a lookup checks: about one page for a B-tree, possibly several levels for an LSM tree. **Space amplification** is stale data waiting for compaction. LSM trees usually win on write throughput and compression; B-trees give more predictable read latency, because compaction competes for I/O and causes spikes. Benchmark your own workload before choosing.

left.title: B-tree
points: Updates pages in place; WAL for crash safety
Point read: ~1 disk read once inner pages are cached
Random writes; whole page written for a small change
Predictable latency, no background compaction
Used by Postgres, InnoDB, SQLite

right.title: LSM tree
points: Append-only: memtable + immutable SSTables
Point read: memtable, then newest to oldest SSTables, with Bloom filters
Sequential writes; high ingest throughput
Compaction rewrites data and can cause p99 spikes
Used by RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra

example.explain: The first table that contains the key wins, so newer values shadow older ones. 'c' has a tombstone in the newer SSTable, so the old value 3 is hidden even though it is still on disk until compaction removes it.

lessons.tryit: Extend the example into a working toy LSM: `put` writes to the memtable; when it holds more than 4 keys, flush it as a sorted list to `sstables[0]`; `delete` writes a tombstone; and `compact()` merges all SSTables into one, keeping only the newest version of each key and dropping tombstones. Write 1,000 random puts and deletes, compare every `get` with a plain dict, and print the write amplification (entries written across all flushes and compactions ÷ entries put).

questions.prompt: How does an LSM tree implement a delete?
options: It finds the SSTable containing the key and rewrites it without the key
It writes a tombstone marker that shadows older values; compaction removes the data later
It removes the key from the Bloom filter
It marks the key's page as free in place
questions.explain: SSTables are immutable, so a delete is a write: a tombstone that reads treat as 'not found'. Rewriting SSTables on every delete would destroy the sequential-write advantage, and standard Bloom filters cannot remove elements.

questions.prompt: Tables are listed newest first and `None` is a tombstone. What does this print?
questions.explain: For 'k' the search stops at the first table containing it, the tombstone, so it returns None, even though an older table still holds 'v1'. 'j' is in the newest table and 'q' is nowhere. Answering 'v1' would mean deleted data comes back.

questions.prompt: An IoT platform ingests 200,000 small writes per second; reads are rare and mostly for recent data. Which storage engine fits best, and why?
options: A B-tree, because reads cost one page
An LSM tree, because it turns random writes into sequential appends and compacts in the background
A B-tree, because it has no write amplification
Either: engines only differ in read performance
questions.explain: The workload is dominated by writes, and an LSM tree absorbs them as memtable inserts plus sequential flushes. A B-tree would do random page writes at 200k/s. B-trees do have write amplification (a whole page per small update), and engines differ mainly on the write side.

questions.prompt: A lookup is for a key that exists in none of 10 SSTables. Each SSTable has a Bloom filter with a 1% false-positive rate. About how many SSTable disk reads does the lookup cost on average?
options: About 0.1
About 1
questions.explain: Each filter says 'maybe' with probability 0.01, triggering a wasted read; 10 × 0.01 = 0.1 reads on average. Without filters it would be 10 reads. It cannot be guaranteed 0, because Bloom filters have false positives (but never false negatives).

video.title: LSM Tree vs B-Tree

lessons.why: Every database is built on one of these two engines. Knowing their trade-offs lets you predict performance and choose the right store for a workload.

terms.d: Fixed-size pages in a balanced tree, updated in place.
Writes go to an in-memory memtable, flushed to sorted immutable SSTables, merged by compaction.
Extra bytes written, pages read and storage used per unit of user data.
A compact structure that says 'definitely not here' to skip SSTables on reads.

mistakes.wrong: LSM trees are always faster.
mistakes.right: They favour writes. Reads may check several files and compaction uses background I/O.

mistakes.wrong: Deleting a key in an LSM tree frees space immediately.
mistakes.right: It writes a tombstone; space is reclaimed only when compaction merges it away.

takeaways: B-trees suit read-heavy workloads with predictable latency.
LSM trees suit write-heavy workloads.
Compare engines by write, read and space amplification.

lessons.title: Write-ahead logs and crash recovery
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain why a log record must be fsynced before a write is acknowledged, and write a replay routine that recovers correctly from a torn final record.
concept: Updating a data structure in place is not crash-safe. Power can fail halfway through writing a 16 KB page (a **torn write**), or between updating a B-tree's parent and child pages, leaving a corrupt structure. The fix is a **write-ahead log** (WAL): before changing any data, append a record describing the change to an append-only file and make it durable; only then acknowledge the client. After a crash, replay the log to redo every acknowledged change. Appends are sequential, so the log is cheap to write.

Durability is about `fsync`, not `write`. A successful `write()` only means the bytes reached the operating system's page cache; a power cut loses them. `fsync()` asks the drive to persist them, which costs anywhere from tens of microseconds (enterprise SSDs with power-loss protection) to several milliseconds (consumer drives). Engines therefore use **group commit**: one fsync covers the records of many concurrent transactions. Each record carries a length and a checksum (for example CRC32), so recovery can recognize a torn final record.

Recovery reads records in order and stops at the first one whose length or checksum is wrong: that is the torn tail, and it was never acknowledged, so dropping it is correct. Records for transactions without a commit marker are ignored. **Checkpoints** bound recovery time: flush the in-memory state, note the log position, and delete older log segments. Raft's persistent state is the same idea: `currentTerm`, `votedFor` and log entries must reach stable storage before a server replies to an RPC.

lessons.tryit: Turn the example into a file-backed store: `put()` appends a record, calls `f.flush()` and `os.fsync(f.fileno())`, then updates a dict. Write a driver that does puts in a loop and prints each acknowledged key, and run it under a parent script that sends `SIGKILL` at a random moment. Restart, replay, and assert that every key printed as acknowledged is present. Then time 10,000 puts with fsync per write against fsync every 100 writes.

questions.prompt: A call to `write(fd, buf, n)` on a regular file returns n. What is guaranteed?
options: The bytes are on the physical disk
The bytes are in the operating system's page cache; a power loss can still lose them
The bytes are on disk unless the disk itself fails
Nothing: write() is asynchronous and may not have copied the buffer
questions.explain: write() copies the data into kernel buffers and returns; the kernel writes back later. Only fsync (or O_DSYNC and similar flags) waits for the device. The buffer has been copied by the time write() returns, so you may reuse it.

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines of a durable `put` for a WAL-backed store, so that a write is never visible or acknowledged before it is on disk.
questions.explain: Encode first, then append, then flush Python's buffer to the OS, then fsync to the device; flush must precede fsync or the bytes are still in user space. Only after fsync may readers see the value in the memtable and the client get 'OK'. Updating the memtable earlier would let a reader see a value that a crash then erases.

questions.prompt: A key/value store acknowledges each write after `write()` and runs `fsync` once per second in a background thread. The machine loses power. What can be lost, and what was gained?
options: Nothing can be lost, because the log is append-only
Up to about one second of acknowledged writes; in exchange, each write avoids waiting for an fsync
Only writes that were not yet acknowledged
The whole log, because the final record is torn
questions.explain: Writes acknowledged since the last fsync were only in the page cache, so up to ~1 s of them disappear (Redis's appendfsync everysec makes this exact trade). Append-only does not imply durable, and recovery truncates only the torn tail, not the whole log.

questions.prompt: A Raft server grants its vote to candidate A in term 7, but keeps `votedFor` only in memory. It crashes, restarts immediately (still in term 7), and receives a RequestVote from candidate B for term 7. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: the restarted server rejects B because it remembers its term
It may vote for B as well, so A and B can both win majorities and term 7 has two leaders
B's request is ignored because restarts always start a new term
The server cannot vote again until it hears a heartbeat
questions.explain: With votedFor forgotten, the server can vote twice in one term, which breaks Raft's one-leader-per-term rule (Election Safety). That is why currentTerm, votedFor and the log are persisted before replying. Restarting does not bump the term, and nothing waits for a heartbeat before voting.

video.title: Write-Ahead Logging in Databases

lessons.why: Crash safety is what makes a database a database. The write-ahead log is how almost every durable system survives power cuts.

terms.d: Append each change to a log before applying it, then replay after a crash.
Forces data from the OS page cache onto stable storage.
A crash in the middle of a write, leaving a partial record.
Batch several transactions into one `fsync` to amortise its cost.

mistakes.wrong: A successful `write()` means the data is on disk.
mistakes.right: It's only in the page cache. Call `fsync` before acknowledging.

mistakes.wrong: Recovery should fail if the last record is corrupt.
mistakes.right: A torn final record was never acknowledged, so stop at it and drop it. Use length and checksum to detect it.

takeaways: Log, fsync, then acknowledge.
Replay records in order and stop at the first invalid one.
Checkpoints bound how much log must be replayed.

lessons.title: Encoding and schema evolution
lessons.objective: By the end you can choose an encoding for a service boundary, hand-encode a protobuf varint, and change a schema without breaking old readers or old writers.
concept: Data in memory must be encoded to bytes before it goes over the network or to disk. Language-specific formats such as Java serialization and Python `pickle` are a trap: they tie you to one language, version poorly, and decoding untrusted input can execute code. JSON is readable and universal but bulky, has no byte-string type, and its numbers are ambiguous: JavaScript parses them as doubles, so integers above 2⁵³ lose precision. Binary formats with schemas (**Protocol Buffers**, Thrift, **Avro**) are compact and come with explicit evolution rules.

During a rolling deploy, old and new code run at the same time, so you need both directions. **Backward compatibility**: new code reads data written by old code. **Forward compatibility**: old code reads data written by new code. Protobuf gets both from **field tags**: each field is encoded as (tag number, wire type, value), and a decoder skips tags it does not know. Renaming a field is free because names never go over the wire; changing a tag number breaks everything. Never reuse a deleted tag (mark it `reserved`), and add new fields with defaults.

Integers are encoded as **varints**: 7 bits per byte, least-significant group first, with the high bit meaning 'more bytes follow'. 300 is binary 1 0010 1100; its low 7 bits 0101100 become 0xAC once the continuation bit is set, and the remaining 10 becomes 0x02, giving `ac 02`. Small numbers take a single byte. Avro takes a different approach: no tags at all, with the reader's and writer's schemas matched by field name, which needs a schema registry. Remember that data outlives code: a row written five years ago is still read today.

Delete a field and reserve its tag
New readers see the default; the tag can never be reused by mistake

Old data decodes as an unknown or a different field
Reuse a deleted tag for a new field

example.explain: Prints `1 01`, `127 7f`, `128 8001`, `300 ac02`. Values up to 127 fit in one byte; 128 needs a continuation byte. This is why protobuf tag numbers 1–15 (one byte, together with the 3-bit wire type) are reserved for frequent fields.

lessons.tryit: Write a `.proto` file for a `User` message (id, name, email), generate code for two languages (or two versions in one language), and serialize a message with v1. Then make v2: delete `email` and reserve tag 3, and add `phone = 4`. Prove both directions: v1 bytes decode with v2 code, and v2 bytes decode with v1 code. Finally, deliberately reuse tag 3 for `phone` and show the corrupted output.

questions.prompt: What does forward compatibility mean?
options: New code can read data written by old code
Old code can read data written by new code
The schema can only grow, never shrink
Data can be converted to the next format version automatically
questions.explain: Forward compatibility is old code tolerating new data, for example by skipping unknown fields. 'New code reads old data' is backward compatibility; you need both during a rolling deploy.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: 150 = 1001 0110 in binary. The low 7 bits are 0010110 (0x16); more bits remain, so the continuation bit is set: 0x96. The remaining value 1 gives 0x01. Big-endian thinking leads to the wrong answer '0196'; varints put the least-significant group first.

questions.prompt: A team deletes `string email = 4;` from a protobuf message, and a month later adds `string phone = 4;`. Old records and old clients are still around. What happens?
options: Nothing: protobuf matches fields by name
Old data that holds email addresses is silently decoded as phone numbers
Decoding fails loudly with a schema mismatch error
Old clients refuse to start
questions.explain: On the wire only the tag 4 and a string wire type are stored, which match exactly, so emails decode as 'phone' with no error. That is the most dangerous kind of bug. The fix is `reserved 4;` and a new tag for phone. Protobuf binary does not use names, so there is no mismatch to detect.

questions.prompt: A Go service returns order IDs like 9007199254740993 as JSON numbers. The JavaScript frontend displays 9007199254740992. What is the cause and the usual fix?
options: A Go bug; upgrade the JSON library
JavaScript numbers are 64-bit doubles that represent integers exactly only up to 2⁵³; send 64-bit IDs as strings
Network corruption; add a checksum
Integer overflow in the frontend; use BigInt arithmetic on the number after parsing
questions.explain: 9007199254740993 is 2⁵³ + 1, the first integer a double cannot represent, so JSON.parse rounds it before your code sees it. Converting to BigInt after parsing is too late; the precision is already gone. Twitter sends both id and id_str for exactly this reason.

lessons.why: Services and stored data outlive any single deploy. Compatible schema evolution lets old and new code run side by side during rollouts.

terms.d: New code can read data written by old code.
Old code can read data written by new code.
Numbers that identify protobuf fields on the wire; names aren't sent.
Integers encoded 7 bits per byte, low group first, high bit meaning 'more follows'.

mistakes.wrong: I can reuse a deleted field's tag number.
mistakes.right: Old data with that tag will be misread. Reserve retired tags forever.

mistakes.wrong: `pickle` is fine for data between services.
mistakes.right: It's Python-only, insecure on untrusted input and fragile across versions. Use JSON, protobuf or Avro.

takeaways: Rolling deploys need both backward and forward compatibility.
Add fields with new tags; never change or reuse tags.
Choose language-neutral encodings for service boundaries.

lessons.title: Replication: leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless
lessons.objective: By the end you can compare the three replication topologies, predict the anomalies replication lag causes, and decide whether a quorum setting (N, W, R) guarantees reading the latest write.
concept: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines, for fault tolerance, read scaling and locality. In **leader-follower** replication (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Kafka) all writes go to one leader, which streams its log to followers. **Synchronous** replication waits for a follower's acknowledgement: durable, but one slow follower blocks writes. **Asynchronous** replication acknowledges immediately: fast, but a failover can lose the newest writes. A common middle ground is semi-synchronous: one follower is synchronous and the rest are asynchronous.

Reads from asynchronous followers show **replication lag** anomalies. Read-your-writes: a user posts a comment, reloads from a lagging follower, and sees nothing. Monotonic reads: two reloads hit different followers and time appears to go backwards. Fixes: read data you recently modified from the leader, or pin each user to one replica. Failover is risky: you detect a dead leader only by timeout, must promote the most up-to-date follower, and must **fence** the old leader so two leaders never accept writes at once (split brain).

**Multi-leader** replication runs a leader in each datacenter, accepts writes locally and replicates between leaders asynchronously. It suits multi-region deployments and offline clients (calendar apps), but concurrent writes to the same record conflict. Resolving them with last-write-wins loses data; merge functions or CRDTs keep it. Collaborative editors such as Google Docs are the extreme case: every client is a leader that keeps working offline and syncs its edits later, which is why they rely on operational transformation or CRDTs.

**Leaderless** replication (Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak): the client sends each write to all N replicas and treats it as successful after W acknowledgements, and reads from R replicas, keeping the newest version. If **W + R > N**, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one node, so a read sees the latest successful write. Stale replicas are fixed by read repair and anti-entropy (Merkle trees). Sloppy quorums with hinted handoff keep writes available during failures, but then the overlap guarantee no longer holds.

One leader per region or device
Yes: needs LWW, merge or CRDTs
Any replica; success after W acks

example.explain: The brute force checks every possible write set against every possible read set. The overlap holds exactly when W + R > N: (3,2,2) and (5,3,3) print True True, while (3,1,1) and (5,2,3) print False False.

lessons.tryit: Simulate a leaderless store with N=3 replicas as dicts of key → (value, version). Implement `write(key, value, W)` that updates a random W replicas and `read(key, R)` that returns the highest version among a random R replicas and repairs stale ones. Run 10,000 write-then-read pairs for each (W, R) in {1,2,3}² and print the fraction of stale reads; confirm it is 0 exactly when W + R > 3.

questions.prompt: In a leaderless store with N = 3, which (W, R) setting guarantees that every read overlaps the latest successful write?
questions.explain: Overlap needs W + R > N, and only 2 + 2 = 4 exceeds 3. The others sum to 2 or 3; with 3 = N, a write to node A and a read from nodes B and C can miss each other.

questions.prompt: A quorum read receives (value, version) from three replicas. It returns the newest value and lists which replicas need read repair. What does this print?
questions.code:
replies = [("v1", 3), ("v2", 7), ("v1", 3)]
newest = max(replies, key=lambda rv: rv[1])
stale = [i for i, rv in enumerate(replies) if rv[1] < newest[1]]
print(newest[0], stale)
questions.explain: Version 7 is the highest, so the read returns v2, and replicas 0 and 2 (still at version 3) get repaired. Taking the majority value (v1 appears twice) is the tempting mistake: quorums compare versions, they do not vote on values.

questions.prompt: An async leader acknowledged writes 1001–1010; its follower has applied up to 1005 when the leader dies. The follower is promoted and starts accepting new writes. When the old leader comes back, what should happen to its writes 1006–1010?
options: They are merged into the new leader automatically
They are discarded: the old leader rejoins as a follower, so those acknowledged writes are lost
The new leader pauses until it receives them
The old leader resumes as leader because it has the longest log
questions.explain: With asynchronous replication, failover loses whatever the follower had not received, even though clients were told 'ok'. Silently merging is dangerous: the new leader may have reused those IDs, which is exactly what happened in GitHub's 2012 MySQL incident. Letting the old leader resume would mean two leaders, which is split brain.

questions.prompt: Writes go to the leader; reads are load-balanced across async followers. Users complain that after changing their profile photo, the page still shows the old one. What is the smallest fix that targets this anomaly?
options: Make every follower synchronous
For about a minute after a user writes, read that user's own profile from the leader
Add more followers
Put a CDN in front of the reads
questions.explain: This is a read-your-writes violation, and you only need to fix it for the writer's own recent data. Fully synchronous replication fixes it but makes every write wait on the slowest follower. More followers or a CDN add more stale copies, not fewer.

resource.title: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store"

video.title: System Design: Database Replication - Multi Leader, Single Leader, Leaderless

lessons.why: Replication keeps data available and close to users, but lag creates anomalies users notice. Each topology makes a different trade-off.

terms.d: One leader takes writes and streams changes to followers.
Followers behind the leader; causes stale and out-of-order reads.
A leader per region accepting writes; conflicts must be resolved.
Write to W and read from R of N replicas; W + R > N makes them overlap.

mistakes.wrong: Reading from any replica is fine after a write.
mistakes.right: A lagging follower may not have it. Route read-your-writes to the leader or a caught-up replica.

mistakes.wrong: W + R > N guarantees linearizable reads.
mistakes.right: It ensures overlap, but sloppy quorums, concurrent writes and failures can still return stale data.

takeaways: Asynchronous replication is fast but can lose recent writes on failover.
Watch for read-your-writes and monotonic-read anomalies.
Multi-leader and leaderless systems need conflict resolution.

lessons.title: Partitioning and consistent hashing
lessons.objective: By the end you can partition a dataset by key range or by hash, calculate how many keys move when a node is added under mod-N and under consistent hashing, and fix a hot partition.
concept: **Partitioning** (sharding) splits data so that each node holds a subset; each partition is then usually replicated. **Key-range** partitioning (Bigtable, HBase, Spanner) keeps keys sorted, so range scans are efficient, but sequential keys such as timestamps send every write to the last partition. **Hash** partitioning spreads keys evenly but destroys order, so a range query must ask every partition. Cassandra combines both: the first part of the primary key is hashed to choose a partition, and the remaining columns are sorted within it.

The naive scheme `hash(key) % N` is a trap. When N changes from 4 to 5, a key stays put only if `h % 4 == h % 5`, which is true for 4 out of every 20 hash values, so 80% of keys move. **Consistent hashing** places nodes and keys on a ring of hash values; a key belongs to the first node clockwise from it. Adding a node takes keys only from its neighbour, so about 1/N of keys move. With few nodes the arcs are uneven, so each physical node gets many **virtual nodes** (for example 100–256 positions), which also spreads a failed node's load across many peers.

Another common scheme fixes many more partitions than nodes, say 1,024 partitions on 10 nodes (Elasticsearch shards, Kafka partitions, Riak), and rebalances by moving whole partitions. No hash function helps with a **hot key**: a celebrity's post read 500,000 times a second lives on one partition. Cache it in front of the store, or split it into sub-keys (`post:42#0` … `post:42#9`) and spread reads across them. Clients find partitions through a routing tier, a client-side partition map, or a coordination service such as ZooKeeper or etcd.

left.title: hash(key) % N
points: One line of code, perfectly even with a good hash
Changing N from 4 to 5 moves ~80% of keys
A cache cluster resize means a near-total cache miss storm
A failed node's keys all need N to change

right.title: Consistent hashing + virtual nodes
points: Ring of hash positions; key goes to the next node clockwise
Adding a 5th node moves ~1/5 of keys
Virtual nodes smooth out uneven arcs
A failed node's load spreads across many peers

example.code:
import bisect, hashlib

def h(s):
    return int(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 2**32

class Ring:
    def __init__(self, nodes, vnodes=100):
        self.ring = sorted((h(f"{n}#{i}"), n) for n in nodes for i in range(vnodes))
        self.points = [p for p, _ in self.ring]

    def owner(self, key):
        i = bisect.bisect(self.points, h(key)) % len(self.ring)
        return self.ring[i][1]

keys = [f"user:{i}" for i in range(10_000)]
before = Ring(["A", "B", "C", "D"])
after = Ring(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"])
moved = sum(before.owner(k) != after.owner(k) for k in keys)
print(f"moved {moved / len(keys):.0%}")
example.explain: MD5 gives a hash that is stable across runs (Python's built-in `hash` of strings is randomized per process). With 100 virtual nodes each, adding a fifth node should move about a fifth of the keys; this run prints `moved 14%` because E's 100 random positions happen to cover a little less than a fifth of the ring. Either way it is far below the 80% that mod-N moves, and more virtual nodes bring the figure closer to 1/5.

lessons.tryit: Run the example, then change `vnodes` to 1, 10 and 1,000. For each, print the share of keys per node (max ÷ mean) and the fraction moved when E is added. Then simulate node B failing: list where B's keys go with 1 virtual node versus 100, and explain in two sentences why virtual nodes prevent one neighbour from doubling its load.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of giving each physical node many virtual nodes on a consistent-hash ring?
options: Fewer hash computations per lookup
Load is spread more evenly, and a failed node's keys spread across many peers instead of one neighbour
Keys can be scanned in sorted order
It removes the need for replication
questions.explain: With one position per node, arcs are uneven and a failed node dumps all its keys on its single successor. Many positions average out the arcs and scatter the failed node's keys. Lookups get slightly more expensive (a bigger sorted array), and ordering is still lost.

questions.prompt: Keys 0–99 are placed with `k % N`. How many of them change nodes when N goes from 4 to 5?
questions.code: print(sum(1 for k in range(100) if k % 4 != k % 5))
questions.explain: k % 4 == k % 5 only when k mod 20 is 0, 1, 2 or 3, which is 4 of every 20 keys, so 20 keys stay and 80 move. Many people guess 20 (the 1/N you get from consistent hashing), but that is what mod-N fails to give you.

questions.prompt: One post's ID gets 500,000 reads per second after a celebrity shares it, and the single partition holding it is overloaded while the rest of the cluster is idle. What helps?
options: Add 10 more nodes to the cluster
Switch from hash to range partitioning
Serve the key from a cache tier, or copy it under several suffixed sub-keys so reads spread across partitions
Change the hash function to MD5
questions.explain: Every request for one key hashes to the same partition, however many nodes you add or whichever hash or partitioning scheme you use. You have to make that one key live in many places: a cache tier, or sub-keys `id#0`…`id#9`, with reads choosing one at random.

questions.prompt: Sensor readings are stored in a range-partitioned store with key = timestamp. Write throughput tops out at one node's capacity no matter how many nodes you add. What is the fix and its cost?
options: Use a bigger node for the last partition; no cost
Prefix the key with the sensor ID (sensor_id, timestamp) so writes spread across partitions; a time-range query over all sensors must now query every partition
Switch to hashing the timestamp; range scans by time stay cheap
Turn off replication on the hot partition
questions.explain: Monotonic keys always hit the newest range, so every write lands on one partition. Prefixing with the sensor ID spreads writes while keeping each sensor's readings sorted, and the price is fan-out for all-sensor queries. Hashing the timestamp also spreads writes, but it destroys time ordering, so time-range scans become full scans.

video.title: What is Consistent Hashing and Where is it used? (ByteByteGo)

lessons.why: Data outgrows one machine. How you partition decides whether adding a node moves 20% of your data or 80%, and whether one hot key melts a server.

terms.d: Contiguous key ranges per node; good for range scans, prone to hot spots.
Spread keys by hash; even load, no efficient range scans.
Adding a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.
One key with so much traffic it overloads its partition.

mistakes.wrong: `hash(key) % N` is a fine way to shard.
mistakes.right: Changing N from 4 to 5 moves about 80% of keys. Use consistent hashing or many fixed partitions.

mistakes.wrong: Even key distribution means even load.
mistakes.right: A single celebrity key can dominate. Split or replicate hot keys.

takeaways: Range partitioning for scans; hash partitioning for even spread.
Virtual nodes smooth out consistent hashing.
Plan for hot keys explicitly.

project.title: LSM-tree key-value store with a WAL
project.brief: Build a single-node key/value store (Go or Rust recommended) with Put, Get, Delete and Scan, backed by a write-ahead log, a memtable, immutable SSTables with Bloom filters, and compaction. It turns this module's ideas into code and gives you a crash-tested storage layer you will reuse under Raft.
milestones: WAL plus in-memory map: every Put and Delete is appended as a [length][crc32][payload] record and fsynced before acknowledging; replay on startup. Test it by running a writer under a script that sends kill -9 at random times, 100 times, and assert that every acknowledged key survives.

Memtable flush: when the memtable exceeds 4 MB, write a sorted, immutable SSTable (data blocks, a sparse index entry every 4 KB, and a footer pointing to the index), record it in a manifest, then start a new WAL.

Read path: memtable, then SSTables newest to oldest, with tombstones honoured; add a Bloom filter per SSTable (target 1% false positives) and report disk reads per lookup for missing keys with and without it.

Compaction: merge SSTables into one in the background, dropping shadowed versions and tombstones, without blocking writes; atomically swap the manifest so a crash mid-compaction leaves the old files valid.

Benchmark 1M random 100-byte writes and 1M random reads: report throughput, p50/p99 latency and write amplification (bytes written to disk ÷ bytes of user data), and plot p99 latency over time to show compaction spikes.
project.stretch: Implement leveled compaction (L0 to Ln with a 10× size ratio) and group commit, then compare write amplification and p99 read latency against your single-merge compaction.

exam.prompt: For N = 3, which (W, R) pairs guarantee read/write overlap? What does this print?
exam.code: print([(w, r) for w in range(1, 4) for r in range(1, 4) if w + r > 3])
exam.explain: The condition W + R > N keeps every pair whose sum is at least 4. Note (1, 3) and (3, 1) qualify: write-one/read-all and write-all/read-one both overlap, but they trade availability for one side (W=3 means any single replica failure blocks writes).

exam.prompt: Your LSM store crashes while flushing a memtable: the new SSTable file is half written and the manifest was not yet updated; the WAL has not been rotated. What should recovery do?
options: Repair the half-written SSTable by scanning it for valid records
Ignore the unlisted SSTable file (delete it) and replay the WAL to rebuild the memtable
Discard the WAL, because the SSTable already holds its data
Refuse to start until an operator intervenes
exam.explain: The manifest is the commit point for SSTables: a file it does not list was never committed. The WAL still holds every acknowledged write, so replaying it reconstructs the memtable exactly. Discarding the WAL would lose data that only the incomplete SSTable contained.

exam.prompt: A cache cluster uses consistent hashing with 3 nodes and one ring position each. Node B fails. What happens to load?
options: B's keys are spread evenly over A and C
All of B's keys move to its single successor, which may double its load and fail next
All keys are reshuffled across A and C
Nothing: requests for B's keys simply fail until B returns
exam.explain: Without virtual nodes, a key's owner is the next node clockwise, so B's whole arc goes to one successor, which can trigger a cascade. With many virtual nodes, B's many small arcs have different successors, so the load spreads. Consistent hashing never reshuffles everything; that is the mod-N problem.

exam.prompt: v2 of a protobuf schema adds `optional string nickname = 7;`. A v1 service receives a v2 message. What happens?
options: Decoding fails because field 7 is not in the v1 schema
The v1 decoder skips (and in current protobuf versions preserves) the unknown field 7 and reads the rest normally
Field 7's bytes are merged into the previous field
The v1 service must be redeployed first
exam.explain: Tags plus wire types tell the decoder how many bytes to skip, so unknown fields are harmless; that is what makes forward compatibility work. Current proto3 implementations keep unknown fields and re-emit them when the message is re-serialized.

exam.prompt: Leaderless store, N = 3, W = 2, R = 2. A write succeeds on nodes A and B; C missed it. Then B's disk dies and B is replaced by an empty node, B'. A client reads from C and B'. What does it see?
options: The latest value, because W + R > N guarantees it
A stale value or nothing: the only surviving copy is on A, and the read missed A
An error, because B' is empty
The latest value, via hinted handoff from A
exam.explain: W + R > N assumes acknowledged writes stay on their nodes. Losing B's data leaves a single copy on A, and {C, B'} does not include A. Anti-entropy (Merkle-tree repair) would eventually copy the value to B', but nothing guarantees it before this read. Hinted handoff covers writes to unavailable nodes, not lost disks.

exam.prompt: Two clients concurrently write different values to the same key in a Dynamo-style store that uses version vectors (lesson s6m1l3's vector clocks). Neither write saw the other. What does the store do?
options: Keeps the write with the later wall-clock timestamp
Detects that the versions are concurrent and keeps both as siblings for the application (or a merge function) to resolve
Rejects the second write
Keeps the write from the replica with the lower node ID
exam.explain: Neither vector dominates the other, so the store knows the writes are concurrent and keeps both rather than guessing. Wall-clock LWW is the alternative that silently loses one; it is not what version vectors are for.

exam.prompt: WAL replay with commit markers: only committed sets are applied. What does this print?
exam.explain: The first transaction (x=1) is committed. The second (x=2, y=5) has no commit marker before the log ends, so it was never acknowledged and must not be applied. Printing {'x': 2, 'y': 5} would expose a transaction that crashed mid-flight.

exam.prompt: A RocksDB-backed service has flat p50 latency but periodic p99 read spikes every few minutes during heavy writes. What is the most likely cause?
options: Bloom filter false positives
Background compaction (and write stalls when it falls behind) competing for disk I/O
WAL replay
Hash collisions in the memtable
exam.explain: Compaction periodically rewrites large amounts of data, saturating I/O, and reads that miss the cache queue behind it; if compaction falls behind, RocksDB also stalls writes. A 1% Bloom false-positive rate adds a constant trickle of reads, not periodic spikes, and WAL replay happens only at startup. Module 4 shows why these tail spikes matter so much.
