modules.summary: The precise guarantees databases offer (and don't), the anomalies that weaker isolation allows, and how 2PC and Raft get machines to agree — ending with a Raft that passes the 6.5840 tests.

lessons.title: Linearizability vs serializability vs eventual consistency
lessons.objective: By the end you can classify a history of concurrent reads and writes as linearizable or not, and explain how linearizability differs from serializability.
concept: **Linearizability** (also called atomic or strong consistency) means the system behaves as if there were one copy of the data, and each operation takes effect atomically at some instant between its start and its response. Consequence: once any read returns a new value, every read that starts later, in real time and from any client, returns that value or a newer one. It is a recency guarantee on a single object. You need it for locks and leader election, uniqueness constraints such as usernames, and cases where two channels (a database and a queue) must agree.

**Serializability** is a different guarantee, about **transactions** over many objects: the result equals some serial order of the transactions, but not necessarily the real-time order. A serializable database may run a read-only transaction against a snapshot from ten seconds ago. **Strict serializability** combines both (serializable, and the order respects real time); Google Spanner calls it external consistency. Mixing the two terms up is the most common mistake in consistency discussions.

**Eventual consistency** only promises that replicas converge if writes stop, with no bound on when and no rule about what reads return in the meantime. Between the extremes sit **causal consistency** (everyone sees causally related writes in order; one of the strongest models that stays available during a partition), read-your-writes and monotonic reads. Stronger models cost latency: a linearizable write must coordinate with a majority, so a cross-region linearizable write costs at least one inter-region round trip.

visual.title: Consistency models at a glance
rows: etcd, ZooKeeper writes, a Raft KV store

example.explain: B's read overlaps the write and returns 1, so the write took effect before B's read finished. C's read starts after B's read ended, so a linearizable system must return 1 to C. Returning 0 is a violation, although eventual consistency would allow it.

lessons.tryit: Write a checker for single-register histories: input a list of operations (client, kind, value, start, end), and output whether some point inside each operation's interval gives a legal sequential order. Brute-force the permutations for histories of up to 6 operations. Test it on the timeline above and on three histories of your own, including one where two reads concurrent with a write return different values (that one is legal).

questions.prompt: Which guarantee is about multi-object transactions and allows the equivalent serial order to differ from real-time order?
options: Linearizability
Serializability
Strict serializability
Read-your-writes
questions.explain: Serializability only requires that some serial order exists. Linearizability is about single objects and real time; strict serializability is both; read-your-writes is a session guarantee for one client.

questions.prompt: write(x=1) runs from t=0 to t=10. Read R1 runs from t=2 to t=4 and returns 1. Read R2 runs from t=5 to t=7 and returns 0. Is this history linearizable?
options: Yes, because both reads overlap the write, so either value is allowed
No: R1 returning 1 means the write took effect by t=4, and R2 starts after that, so it must return 1
Yes, if R1 and R2 come from different clients
No, because a read can never return a value before the write completes
questions.explain: Each read on its own could return 0 or 1, since both overlap the write. But R1 pins the write's effect to before t=4, and R2 starts at t=5, so 'new then old' is impossible in a single copy. Reads concurrent with a write may return the new value early, and this applies whichever clients issue them.

questions.prompt: An upload service stores an image in a replicated object store, then puts 'resize image 42' on a queue. The resize worker fetches image 42 and gets 'not found', but a retry seconds later works. Which guarantee is missing?
options: Serializability of the queue
Linearizability of the object store: the worker read a replica that had not yet received the write
Durability of the object store
Exactly-once delivery from the queue
questions.explain: There are two channels (store and queue), and the message raced ahead of replication. A linearizable store would make the write visible to any read that starts after the write completed. The image was not lost (the retry finds it), and the queue delivered correctly.

questions.prompt: Which of these features genuinely needs a linearizable operation?
options: Showing the number of likes on a post
Ensuring two users cannot register the same username
Displaying a product recommendation carousel
Computing yesterday's revenue for a dashboard
questions.explain: Uniqueness needs every node to agree on whether a name is taken at the moment of the claim; a linearizable compare-and-set does it. Like counts, recommendations and yesterday's revenue can be slightly stale without harm.

lessons.why: 'Consistent' means different things in different systems. Knowing the models precisely tells you what a database actually promises.

terms.d: Behaves like one copy; each operation takes effect at one instant between its start and end.
Transactions give the result of some serial order, not necessarily real-time order.
Serializable and consistent with real time.
Replicas converge if writes stop, with no bound on when.

mistakes.wrong: Serializable and linearizable mean the same thing.
mistakes.right: Serializability is about transactions over many objects; linearizability is about single operations in real time.

mistakes.wrong: Eventual consistency means data is correct within a few seconds.
mistakes.right: It gives no time bound and no rules for reads in the meantime.

takeaways: Linearizability = one copy, real-time order.
Serializability = some serial order of transactions.
Ask what a database guarantees, not whether it's 'consistent'.

lessons.title: CAP and PACELC: what CAP actually says
lessons.objective: By the end you can state the CAP theorem precisely, explain why 'pick two of three' is misleading, and describe a database's behaviour with PACELC.
concept: CAP (Brewer's conjecture, 2000, proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002) is narrower than its reputation. It says: when a network **partition** separates nodes, a system cannot provide both **linearizability** (C) and **availability**, meaning every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response. Partitions are not optional in real networks, so the actual choice is what to do during one: some nodes refuse or wait (keeping C), or every node answers, possibly with stale data (keeping A). 'CA' is not a real option for a distributed system.

CAP is silent about almost everything you care about: it considers one consistency model (linearizability), one kind of fault (a partition), and nothing about latency or normal operation. Many real systems are neither CAP-consistent nor CAP-available. A Raft store is unavailable on the minority side of a partition. A single-leader database with asynchronous follower reads is not linearizable. That is why Martin Kleppmann argues against labelling databases 'CP' or 'AP' at all.

**PACELC** (Daniel Abadi, 2010) fills the gap: if there is a **P**artition, choose **A**vailability or **C**onsistency; **E**lse, in normal operation, choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency. The else-branch matters more day to day, because partitions are rare but every request pays latency. Cassandra at consistency ONE is PA/EL: it answers fast and accepts stale reads. etcd, ZooKeeper and Spanner are PC/EC: they wait for a majority. Many systems let you tune this per request, for example Cassandra's QUORUM versus ONE.

visual.title: During a partition: keep C or keep A

left.title: Choose consistency (PC)
points: The minority side rejects or blocks requests
Clients see errors and timeouts, never stale data
The majority side keeps serving linearizably
etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner, your Raft KV store

right.title: Choose availability (PA)

Reads may be stale; writes may conflict

lessons.tryit: Pick a database you use at work or in projects (Postgres with replicas, MongoDB, DynamoDB, Redis, Cassandra…). Write half a page answering: what happens to reads and writes on each side of a partition between the primary and a replica? What consistency do reads get in normal operation with the default settings? Which settings change that, and at what latency cost? Back every claim with a link to the official documentation.

questions.prompt: In the CAP theorem, what does 'C' mean?
options: ACID consistency: transactions preserve invariants
Linearizability: the system behaves like a single up-to-date copy
Eventual convergence of replicas
Durability of committed writes
questions.explain: Gilbert and Lynch's proof uses linearizability (atomic consistency). The 'C' in ACID is a different idea: application invariants. Mixing the two is a classic confusion.

questions.prompt: A 5-node etcd cluster is partitioned into a group of 3 and a group of 2. A client connected to a node in the 2-node group issues a write. What happens?
options: The write succeeds locally and syncs after the partition heals
The write cannot commit, because 2 nodes are not a majority of 5; the client gets an error or timeout
The 2-node group elects its own leader and commits
The write is redirected across the partition to the leader
questions.explain: A commit needs 3 of 5 nodes. The minority cannot elect a leader (it needs 3 votes) and cannot reach the majority's leader, because the partition blocks exactly that path. Accepting the write locally would make the system available but not linearizable, which etcd will not do.

questions.prompt: A vendor says their distributed database is 'CA: consistent and available'. What is the best response?
options: Great, that is the ideal combination
Ask what happens when a partition occurs: either some requests fail (not available) or nodes can diverge (not consistent); 'CA' only describes a system that never sees a partition
CA is only possible with synchronous replication, so check that it is enabled
CA means it is a single-node database, which is always fine
questions.explain: Networks partition, so a distributed system must behave somehow when they do; 'CA' just leaves that behaviour unspecified. Synchronous replication makes a partition stall writes, so the system gives up availability. A single-node database is not distributed, so CAP does not apply to it.

questions.prompt: The shopping-cart team says: 'Adding an item must never fail, even if a region is cut off; a briefly stale cart is fine.' Which PACELC posture fits, and what is the known side effect?
options: PC/EC; carts may reject adds during partitions
PA/EL with merge on conflict (union of cart versions); a deleted item can reappear after a merge
PC/EL; reads are fast but writes block during partitions
PA/EC; impossible combinations are rejected by the store
questions.explain: Never failing an add means choosing availability during a partition, and tolerating staleness means low latency otherwise: PA/EL. Dynamo's cart merges concurrent versions by union, which preserves every add but can resurrect removed items. PC postures fail or block adds during partitions, which contradicts the requirement.

lessons.why: CAP is quoted constantly and often wrongly. Stating it precisely, and using PACELC for normal operation, lets you describe real databases honestly.

terms.d: During a partition, a system can be linearizable or available, not both.
A network failure that splits nodes into groups that can't communicate.
Every request to a non-failed node gets a response.
If Partition, choose A or C; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.

mistakes.wrong: CAP means pick any two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance.
mistakes.right: Partitions happen whether you like it or not. The choice is C or A during a partition.

mistakes.wrong: CAP covers the trade-offs I care about day to day.
mistakes.right: It ignores latency and normal operation. PACELC adds the latency/consistency trade-off.

Most of the time the real trade-off is latency vs consistency.

lessons.title: Transactions and isolation anomalies
lessons.objective: By the end you can spot dirty reads, lost updates, read skew and write skew in an interleaving, and choose the isolation level or locking pattern that prevents each.
concept: ACID: **atomicity** (all or nothing, so you can abort and retry), **consistency** (application invariants, which are really your job), **isolation** (concurrent transactions don't interfere) and **durability**. Full isolation is expensive, so databases offer levels. **Read committed** (the Postgres default) prevents dirty reads and dirty writes. **Snapshot isolation** gives each transaction a consistent snapshot through MVCC (Postgres calls it REPEATABLE READ). **Serializable** behaves as if transactions ran one at a time, implemented with two-phase locking or, in Postgres, serializable snapshot isolation (SSI).

Anomalies to recognize: a **dirty read** sees another transaction's uncommitted data. A **lost update** happens when two read-modify-write cycles interleave: both read likes = 10, both write 11, and one increment vanishes. Prevent it with atomic updates (`UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1`), `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, or compare-and-set. **Read skew** is a transaction seeing different parts of the database at different moments, like a backup that catches money mid-transfer; snapshot isolation prevents it.

**Write skew** is the subtle one: two transactions read the same data, make a decision, then write **different** rows, and together break an invariant. A hospital requires at least one doctor on call. Alice and Bob each check that two doctors are on call, and each takes themself off: zero remain. Snapshot isolation does not catch this, because the two transactions never write the same row. Fixes: SERIALIZABLE isolation, or lock the rows you read with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`. When the conflicting rows don't exist yet (two bookings for one room slot), you get a **phantom**, and only serializable isolation or a materialized lock row helps.

db = {"likes": 10}
# Two transactions interleave their read-modify-write cycles
t1_read = db["likes"]        # T1 reads 10
t2_read = db["likes"]        # T2 reads 10
db["likes"] = t1_read + 1    # T1 writes 11
db["likes"] = t2_read + 1    # T2 writes 11: T1's increment is lost
print(db["likes"])           # 11, not 12

# The fix pushes the read-modify-write into the database as one atomic step:
# UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 WHERE id = 42;
example.explain: Each transaction computed its new value from a stale read, so the second write overwrote the first. An atomic UPDATE makes the database do the read and the write under one row lock, so the two increments run one after the other.

questions.prompt: Which anomaly is NOT prevented by snapshot isolation?
options: Dirty read
Read skew
Write skew
Non-repeatable read
questions.explain: Snapshot isolation gives every transaction one consistent snapshot, which removes dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and read skew. Write skew involves writes to different rows, so the snapshot engine's write-write conflict check never fires.

questions.prompt: Two doctors are on call. Each transaction reads its own snapshot, checks that at least 2 are on call, then takes its doctor off. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both checks read their snapshots, which still show two doctors, so both updates happen and zero doctors remain on call: write skew. Answering 1 assumes Bob's check sees Alice's change, which is what serializable isolation (or FOR UPDATE locks) would enforce.

questions.prompt: Checkout runs `SELECT stock FROM items WHERE id = 7` (gets 1), checks stock > 0 in application code, then runs `UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7`. Under read committed, two concurrent buyers both get stock = 1. What happens, and what is the simplest correct fix?

Both decrement, stock becomes -1 and the item is oversold; fix it with `UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND stock > 0` and check that one row was updated
One update is lost, so stock is 0 and both orders succeed; fix it with a bigger connection pool
The database deadlocks; fix it by retrying
questions.explain: Each decrement is atomic, so no update is lost, but the check happened on a stale read, so the invariant breaks. Putting the condition in the UPDATE makes the check and the write one atomic step: the second buyer's UPDATE matches 0 rows. There is no deadlock here, just two serialized row updates.

`UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = 1`
Two separate transactions: one to read, one to write
`SELECT n FROM counters WHERE id = 1` with a retry loop
questions.explain: The atomic UPDATE reads and writes the row under its row lock, so a concurrent increment waits and then sees the new value. Every other option computes the new value from a read that another transaction can invalidate before the write.

lessons.title: Two-phase commit
lessons.objective: By the end you can walk through 2PC's prepare and commit phases, identify its two points of no return, and explain why a coordinator crash after prepare leaves participants blocked.
concept: A transaction that debits an account on shard 1 and credits one on shard 2 must commit on both or on neither: **atomic commit**. In **two-phase commit**, the coordinator first sends PREPARE to every participant. Each participant durably writes the transaction's changes and a 'prepared' record to its WAL, keeps its locks, and votes YES (a promise: 'I can commit no matter what, even after a crash') or NO. If every vote is YES, the coordinator durably logs COMMIT, which is **the commit point**, and then tells everyone; otherwise it logs and sends ABORT.

There are two points of no return. Once a participant votes YES, it may no longer abort on its own. Once the coordinator logs its decision, the outcome is fixed. Now suppose the coordinator crashes after collecting YES votes but before the participants hear the outcome. They are **in doubt**: they cannot commit (someone might have voted NO) and cannot abort (the coordinator might have logged COMMIT and told someone). They keep holding locks until the coordinator recovers and reads its log. That is why 2PC is called a **blocking** protocol.

In practice, XA transactions spanning different systems (a database and a message broker) are fragile: in-doubt transactions hold row locks and can stall a database, and operators sometimes resolve them by hand, breaking atomicity. Spanner and CockroachDB run 2PC where every participant and the coordinator is itself a Paxos or Raft group, so a single crashed machine cannot block the protocol. Microservices often use **sagas** instead: a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, which gives up isolation. Note that two-phase commit (2PC) and two-phase locking (2PL) are unrelated.

steps.detail: Sent to every participant

steps.label: Participants: prepare
steps.detail: Write changes + 'prepared' to WAL, fsync, keep locks

steps.label: Participants: vote
steps.detail: YES = promise to commit, even after a crash

example.code:
def decide(votes):
    # votes: participant -> "yes", "no", or None (no reply before the timeout)
    if all(v == "yes" for v in votes.values()):
        return "COMMIT"
    return "ABORT"

# The coordinator may abort on a missing vote, because nobody has been told COMMIT.
print(decide({"shard1": "yes", "shard2": None}))   # ABORT
print(decide({"shard1": "yes", "shard2": "yes"}))  # COMMIT (log it durably before sending)
example.explain: Before the decision, a timeout is safe to treat as NO: the coordinator can still abort. After a participant has voted YES, that participant has lost the option to time out and abort; only the coordinator's logged decision can release it.

lessons.tryit: Simulate 2PC with one coordinator and three participants as Python objects that write to per-node log lists. Add crash points: after any participant's prepare, after the coordinator's decision log, and after sending to only one participant. For each crash point, write the recovery rule (what the node reads from its own log and what it does) and assert that every participant ends with the same outcome after recovery.

questions.prompt: What is the commit point in two-phase commit?
options: When the first participant votes YES
When the coordinator durably records its COMMIT decision
When the last participant acknowledges COMMIT
When the client receives 'ok'
questions.explain: Once the decision is on the coordinator's stable storage, the transaction is committed: recovery will re-send COMMIT until every participant has applied it. YES votes are only promises; the final acks and the client reply come after the outcome is already fixed.

questions.prompt: Arrange a participant's PREPARE handler so that a YES vote is only sent once the promise is durable.
questions.explain: A participant that cannot commit votes NO immediately. Otherwise it must write the prepared record and fsync before voting YES: if it crashed after a non-durable YES, it could wake up with no record of its promise and abort a transaction the coordinator then commits.

questions.prompt: Participant P2 voted YES. Then the network between P2 and the coordinator partitions, and P2's wait for the decision times out. What may P2 safely do?
options: Abort after the timeout, because the coordinator is probably dead
Commit after the timeout, because it voted YES
Keep waiting with its locks held; it may ask other participants, and if one knows the outcome (or voted NO) follow that
Delete its prepared record and forget the transaction
questions.explain: After voting YES, P2 cannot decide alone: the coordinator may have committed (so aborting breaks atomicity) or aborted (so committing breaks it). Asking peers can resolve it only if a peer learned the decision or voted NO, which proves the outcome was abort. Otherwise it blocks, and that is 2PC's fundamental weakness.

questions.prompt: The coordinator receives YES from every participant, then crashes before writing its decision to its log. When it recovers, it finds a record of the transaction but no decision. What is correct?
options: Commit, since all votes were YES
Abort: no decision was logged, so no participant can have been told COMMIT
Ask the client what it wants
Leave the transaction in doubt forever
questions.explain: The coordinator only sends COMMIT after logging it, so no decision in the log means nobody heard COMMIT, and aborting is safe (this is the 'presumed abort' rule). Committing would also be safe in this exact case, but the coordinator cannot know the votes were all YES unless it logged them, and the standard, simplest rule is to abort. The client has no say in atomic commit.

Each participant makes the change durable and promises it can commit.
The coordinator logging its decision; after that the outcome is fixed.
A participant that voted yes but hasn't heard the decision; it must wait.

mistakes.wrong: If the coordinator crashes, participants can just abort.
mistakes.right: After voting yes they can't decide alone; aborting could contradict a commit decision. They block.

mistakes.wrong: 2PC is a consensus algorithm.
mistakes.right: It needs every participant and blocks on coordinator failure. Consensus tolerates a minority failing.

takeaways: Two points of no return: the yes vote and the logged decision.
2PC blocks while the coordinator is down.
Sagas use compensating actions instead of distributed locks.

lessons.title: Raft: leader election, log replication, safety
lessons.objective: By the end you can simulate Raft's election and log replication for a 5-node cluster on paper, including a network partition, and state the rules that keep committed entries safe.
concept: Raft (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014) replicates a log so that a cluster of 2f+1 servers behaves like one state machine and survives f failures. Time is divided into **terms**, numbered upward, each with at most one leader. A server is a follower, a candidate or the leader. A follower that hears no heartbeat (an AppendEntries RPC, possibly empty) within its randomized **election timeout** becomes a candidate: it increments `currentTerm`, votes for itself, persists that, and sends RequestVote to every peer. The 6.5840 tester allows at most ten heartbeats per second, so use timeouts of several hundred milliseconds.

A server grants at most one vote per term, and only if the candidate's log is **at least as up-to-date** as its own: a higher last log term, or the same last term and a last index at least as large. A candidate with votes from a majority becomes leader and immediately sends heartbeats. Any server that sees a higher term in any RPC or reply adopts that term and becomes a follower. Randomized timeouts make split votes rare, and a split vote simply leads to a new election in the next term.

The leader appends each client command to its log and sends AppendEntries with `prevLogIndex` and `prevLogTerm`. A follower rejects the RPC if its log has no entry at prevLogIndex with that term; the leader then backs up `nextIndex` and retries, and conflicting follower entries are deleted, so followers converge on the leader's log. An entry is **committed** once it is stored on a majority **and** it belongs to the leader's current term (older entries become committed indirectly). Committed entries are applied to the state machine in index order.

Raft's safety properties: at most one leader per term; a leader never overwrites its own log; if two logs share an entry with the same index and term, they are identical up to it; and every committed entry is present in every future leader's log, because the up-to-date check prevents a server missing it from winning a majority. Persist `currentTerm`, `votedFor` and `log[]` before replying to any RPC. During a partition, an old leader on the minority side may keep accepting commands, but it can never commit them.

steps.detail: No heartbeat within a random timeout

steps.label: Become candidate
steps.detail: currentTerm++, votedFor = self, persist

steps.label: RequestVote to all
steps.detail: Carries term, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm

steps.label: Peers vote
steps.detail: One vote per term, only for an up-to-date log

steps.label: Majority: leader
steps.detail: Send heartbeats now; otherwise time out and retry in term+1

example.explain: The handler first adopts any higher term, then grants the vote only if this term's vote is still free (or already given to this candidate) and the candidate's log is up to date. Persisting before replying and resetting the timer only on a grant are the two details most lab bugs come from.

Which servers can win the next election, and in which term? Send two client commands to S1 and one to the new leader, heal the partition, and write out every server's log after the AppendEntries exchanges. Mark which entries were committed and which were overwritten.

questions.prompt: Which Raft state must be on stable storage before a server responds to an RPC?
options: commitIndex and lastApplied
currentTerm, votedFor and log[]
nextIndex[] and matchIndex[]
The election timeout value
questions.explain: Figure 2 of the Raft paper lists currentTerm, votedFor and log[] as persistent state. commitIndex and lastApplied are volatile and rebuilt after a restart; nextIndex and matchIndex are volatile leader state, reinitialized after every election.

questions.prompt: This is Raft's 'at least as up-to-date' check. What does it print?
questions.explain: In the first call the candidate's last term (3) beats the voter's (2), so the candidate wins even though its log is shorter (5 vs 9): term comparison comes first. In the second call the terms tie, so the longer log wins and 5 < 6 means no vote. Comparing lengths first is the classic bug.

questions.prompt: A 5-node cluster has leader S1 in term 4. A partition splits it into {S1, S2} and {S3, S4, S5}. Clients keep talking to both sides. What happens?
options: S1 keeps committing writes, because it is still the leader
S1 accepts commands but cannot commit them; S3–S5 elect a leader in term 5 and commit new entries; when the partition heals, S1 sees term 5, steps down, and its uncommitted entries are overwritten
Both sides elect leaders in term 5 and merge their logs after healing
The whole cluster stops until the partition heals
questions.explain: Committing needs 3 of 5 replicas, which S1's side cannot reach, but nothing stops S1 from appending to its own log. The majority side can elect a new leader in a higher term. The minority side cannot elect anyone (it needs 3 votes), and Raft never merges divergent logs; the leader's log wins.

questions.prompt: A new leader in term 5 finds that an entry from term 3 is now stored on a majority of servers. Why may it not mark that entry committed just by counting replicas?
options: Because entries from earlier terms are always discarded
Because a server holding a log whose last entry has a higher term could still win an election and overwrite it; the leader commits it indirectly by committing a term-5 entry after it
Because commitIndex can only increase by one at a time
Because only the original term-3 leader may commit it
questions.explain: This is Figure 8 in the Raft paper. A majority copy of an old-term entry can still be overwritten by a candidate whose log ends in a newer term. Once a current-term entry is on a majority, no server without it can be elected, so it and every entry before it are safe. Old entries are not discarded, and commitIndex can jump by many entries at once.

Randomised wait after which a follower becomes a candidate.
Higher last term, or same last term and at least as long; required to win votes.
Stored on a majority by the current leader; never lost.

mistakes.wrong: A leader can commit an entry as soon as it's on a majority, whatever its term.
mistakes.right: A leader only commits entries from its own term by counting replicas; earlier entries commit indirectly.

mistakes.wrong: Raft works with any number of servers surviving.
mistakes.right: It needs a majority. Five servers tolerate two failures.

Votes go only to candidates with up-to-date logs, so leaders hold all committed entries.

project.title: Raft (MIT 6.5840 Lab 3)
project.brief: Implement Raft in Go in the 6.5840 skeleton, covering leader election, log replication, persistence and log compaction, until all of the 3A–3D tests pass repeatedly under -race. This is the module's core skill: the protocol, plus the discipline to debug a concurrent, failure-injected system.
milestones: Read the extended Raft paper twice, focusing on Figure 2, and write a one-page summary of every rule in your own words before writing code.

3A leader election: RequestVote, empty AppendEntries heartbeats (at most ten per second), randomized election timeouts and step-down on higher terms; pass `make RUN="-run 3A" raft1` 50 times in a row.

3B log replication: Start(), the AppendEntries consistency check with prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm, nextIndex/matchIndex, the current-term majority commit rule, and an applier goroutine that sends ApplyMsg strictly in order; pass 3B.

3C persistence: persist currentTerm, votedFor and the log through the Persister on every change, and add fast log backtracking (conflict term and index in the reply) so the unreliable Figure 8 tests finish in time; pass 3C.

3D log compaction: Snapshot(), the InstallSnapshot RPC, and index translation after trimming the log; then run the full 3A–3D suite at least 500 times with a parallel test runner and -race, and fix every flaky failure.
project.stretch: Build Lab 4 on top of your Raft: a fault-tolerant key/value service with duplicate detection by (clientId, seq), checked for linearizability by the lab's porcupine-based tests, and measure throughput with 3 vs 5 servers.

exam.prompt: A client is connected to an old Raft leader on the minority side of a partition. It sends Put(x, 5). What does the client experience, and what must the client library do?
options: Put succeeds immediately; nothing extra is needed

The Put is appended but never committed, so the client times out; it must retry against other servers with the same (clientId, seq) so the KV service can drop a duplicate if the first attempt ever commits
The Put fails with a 'not leader' error at once, and retrying is unsafe
The old leader forwards the Put across the partition
exam.explain: A minority leader cannot commit, so it never replies 'ok', and the client sees a timeout with an unknown outcome (module 1). The request might yet commit if this leader regains a majority before its entry is overwritten, so retries need idempotency via (clientId, seq). The old leader does not know it has been deposed, so it does not send 'not leader', and forwarding across a partition is impossible.

exam.prompt: Arrange a leader's commit-advance routine: find the highest index N above commitIndex that is replicated on a majority and comes from the current term. `match_index` includes the leader itself.
lines: replicas = sum(1 for m in match_index if m >= n)
if replicas * 2 > len(match_index) and log[n].term == current_term:
exam.explain: Scan downward from the newest entry, count servers whose matchIndex reaches n, and commit the first n with a strict majority and the current term (the Figure 8 rule). If none qualifies, commitIndex stays where it was, which is why that return sits after the loop.

exam.prompt: What does this print (majority sizes for clusters of 3, 4, 5 and 7)?
exam.explain: A majority is floor(n/2) + 1. Note that 4 nodes need 3 votes, so they tolerate only 1 failure, the same as 3 nodes. That is why consensus clusters use odd sizes: the fourth node adds cost and latency but no fault tolerance.

exam.prompt: A booking app checks `SELECT count(*) FROM bookings WHERE room = 5 AND slot = '10:00'` (gets 0), then inserts a booking, under snapshot isolation. Two users do this concurrently and both succeed. What is the anomaly, and which fix works?
options: Lost update; use an atomic increment
A phantom (write skew via inserts); use SERIALIZABLE isolation or a unique constraint on (room, slot)
Dirty read; use read committed
Read skew; use snapshot isolation
exam.explain: Both transactions read an empty result, then insert new rows that the other's query would have matched: a phantom. `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` cannot lock rows that don't exist yet, so use a unique index, SERIALIZABLE isolation, or a pre-created slot row to lock. The transactions are already at snapshot isolation, so that cannot be the fix.

exam.prompt: Your 6.5840 KV service runs on Raft with every operation, including reads, going through the log. During a 3|2 partition, what do clients of servers on the 2-node side get, and how is that described in CAP and PACELC terms?
options: Stale reads but successful writes: PA/EL
Neither reads nor writes complete on the minority side, while the majority side stays linearizable: it gives up availability, PC/EC
Both sides serve reads and writes, and conflicts are merged afterwards
Reads succeed from the local copy, which keeps it linearizable
exam.explain: Reads through the log need a commit, which needs a majority, so the minority side cannot serve anything; that keeps linearizability at the cost of availability. Serving local reads on the minority side would return stale data and break linearizability. Even without a partition, every operation waits for a majority round trip: EC.

exam.prompt: A Raft follower appends entries to an in-memory log and replies success to AppendEntries, but writes to disk only every 100 ms. Why is this unsafe? (Connects to module 2's WAL lesson.)
options: It is safe, because the leader keeps a copy of everything

The leader counts that reply toward a majority and may commit; if the follower and the leader then crash, the committed entry may survive on fewer than a majority and a new leader can be elected without it
It is only slow, not unsafe
Followers never need to persist, only leaders
exam.explain: Commitment means 'on stable storage on a majority'. An acknowledgement backed only by memory turns a power loss into a lost committed entry, the same 'acknowledge before fsync' bug as in a WAL. The leader's copy does not help if the leader also fails, and a new leader is elected from the survivors.

exam.prompt: Postgres runs at SERIALIZABLE. The app writes a row on the primary and then immediately reads it from an asynchronous read replica, which returns the old value. Which guarantee did the read violate?
options: Serializability
Linearizability (and read-your-writes), not serializability: some serial order still explains the history
Durability
Atomicity
exam.explain: Serializability lets a read-only transaction be ordered before the write, so a stale read is allowed. What the user expects is recency, which is linearizability or at least read-your-writes, and an async replica does not provide it. The write is durable and atomic on the primary.

exam.prompt: What is the essential difference between what 2PC and Raft solve?
options: 2PC replicates one log; Raft commits transactions across shards
2PC gets different participants holding different data to agree on one commit/abort decision and needs every one of them; Raft replicates the same log and needs only a majority
They are interchangeable
Raft is blocking and 2PC is not
exam.explain: Atomic commit needs every participant, since each holds a different part of the transaction; consensus over a replicated log needs a majority, since every replica holds the same data. That is why Spanner layers 2PC over Raft or Paxos groups. 2PC is the blocking protocol, not Raft.

lessons.title: Async I/O and event loops (epoll)
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how an event loop uses epoll to serve 10,000 connections on one thread, predict how a small asyncio program interleaves, and spot code that blocks the loop.
concept: Thread-per-connection is simple, but each thread costs memory (Linux reserves 8 MB of virtual stack by default; tens of KB are actually resident) plus scheduling and context switches. At 10,000 to 100,000 mostly idle connections (the **C10K problem**) that overhead dominates. The alternative is non-blocking sockets plus **readiness notification**: one thread asks the kernel which of its 10,000 sockets are readable or writable right now, and only touches those.

`select` and `poll` pass the whole set of file descriptors on every call, which costs O(n). Linux **epoll** registers interest once (`epoll_ctl`), and `epoll_wait` returns only the ready descriptors, which costs O(ready). BSD and macOS use kqueue, and Windows has completion-based IOCP. **io_uring** (Linux 5.1+) submits I/O through rings shared with the kernel. In **edge-triggered** mode epoll reports only changes, so you must read until `EAGAIN`; in **level-triggered** mode (the default) it keeps reporting a socket as long as data remains.

An event loop (nginx, Redis, Node.js's libuv, Python's asyncio) repeats one cycle: wait for ready events, run the callbacks or resume the coroutines waiting on them until each awaits again, then run expired timers. The golden rule is **never block the loop**: a 50 ms CPU-bound JSON parse or a synchronous database call stalls every other connection for 50 ms. Move CPU-heavy work to a thread or process pool. Go hides all this: goroutines look blocking, but the runtime's netpoller uses epoll underneath and parks goroutines cheaply.

example.code:
import asyncio

async def handle(reader, writer):
    while data := await reader.readline():   # yields to the loop while waiting
        writer.write(data.upper())
        await writer.drain()                 # back-pressure: wait if the send buffer is full
    writer.close()

async def main():
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, "127.0.0.1", 8888)
    async with server:
        await server.serve_forever()

asyncio.run(main())
example.explain: One thread serves every connection: each `await` hands control back to the loop, which uses epoll (on Linux) to resume whichever connection has data. `drain()` pauses a writer whose client reads slowly instead of buffering without limit.

Interest is registered once and epoll_wait returns only ready descriptors, so each call costs O(ready), not O(all)
epoll makes reads non-blocking automatically
epoll uses multiple threads internally
questions.explain: select and poll copy and scan every descriptor on every call. epoll keeps the interest set in the kernel and hands back only what is ready. Both work with any socket type, and non-blocking mode is a separate socket flag.

questions.prompt: Two coroutines yield to the event loop after each step. What does this print?

import asyncio

log = []

async def worker(name, n):
    for i in range(n):
        log.append(f"{name}{i}")
        await asyncio.sleep(0)

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(worker("A", 2), worker("B", 3))
    print(" ".join(log))

asyncio.run(main())

questions.prompt: A Node.js API's p99 latency jumps from 20 ms to 900 ms after a new endpoint starts hashing passwords with synchronous bcrypt (about 100 ms of CPU per call). Other endpoints slow down too. Why, and what is the fix?

bcrypt leaks memory; restart the process hourly
The network is saturated; enable compression

The kernel buffer overflowed

lessons.title: Back-pressure and queues
lessons.objective: By the end you can use Little's law and utilization to predict queue size and wait time, and choose between bounded buffering, back-pressure, load shedding and a durable log for an overloaded pipeline.
concept: A queue absorbs bursts; it does not add capacity. If the arrival rate λ exceeds the service rate μ for long enough, the queue grows without bound: with λ = 1,200/s and μ = 1,000/s it grows by 200 items every second, 720,000 after an hour, and every new item waits behind all of them. An unbounded queue turns overload into huge latency and then an out-of-memory crash. As Fred Hébert puts it, queues don't fix overload.

**Little's law**: L = λ × W, where L is the average number of items in the system, λ the arrival rate and W the average time each spends inside. It holds for any stable system. At 500 requests/s with 200 ms average latency, 100 requests are in flight, which tells you how many threads or connections you need. Queueing theory adds the hard part: as utilization ρ = λ/μ approaches 1, waiting explodes. In an M/M/1 queue, time in the system is 1/(1−ρ) times the service time: 2× at 50% busy, 10× at 90% and 100× at 99%. Keep headroom.

When load exceeds capacity, choose deliberately. **Back-pressure**: bound the queue and make producers slow down when it is full (TCP flow control, Go's buffered channels, Reactive Streams). **Load shedding**: reject quickly with 429 or 503, lowest priority first, because a cheap rejection keeps the server healthy for the requests it accepts. **Durable log**: if the work can wait, write it to Kafka and process it later. Enforce per-client limits at the edge with a token bucket. Bound every queue, monitor its depth and time-in-queue, and drop requests whose deadline has already passed.

example.code:
class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate, capacity):
        self.rate, self.capacity = rate, capacity
        self.tokens, self.last = capacity, 0.0

    def allow(self, now):
        # refill for the time elapsed, never above capacity
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False

b = TokenBucket(rate=2, capacity=3)          # 2 req/s sustained, bursts of up to 3
print([b.allow(t) for t in (0, 0, 0, 0, 0.5, 0.6, 2.0)])
example.explain: The bucket starts full, so three requests at t=0 pass and the fourth is rejected. By t=0.5 one token has refilled; at t=0.6 only 0.2 tokens exist, so that request is refused; by t=2.0 the bucket has refilled to its cap of 3. Output: [True, True, True, False, True, False, True].

Average items in the system = arrival rate × average time in the system
Latency grows linearly with utilization
A queue's length equals its service rate

Bound the queue and slow producers when it's full.

mistakes.right: A queue absorbs bursts. If arrivals exceed service rate for long, it grows without bound.

lessons.title: Caching strategies and invalidation
lessons.objective: By the end you can choose between cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-behind for a workload, compute effective latency from a hit rate, and prevent stale sets and stampedes.
concept: A cache trades freshness for speed: a Redis or memcached GET in the same datacenter takes well under a millisecond, while a database query often takes 5–50 ms. Effective latency is `h × t_hit + (1 − h) × t_miss`. With 1 ms hits and 50 ms misses, a 90% hit rate gives 5.9 ms and 99% gives 1.49 ms. Going from 90% to 99% also cuts database load from 10% of requests to 1%, a tenfold drop. Small hit-rate gains are worth a lot.

Four patterns. **Cache-aside**, the most common: the app reads the cache, and on a miss reads the database and fills the cache. **Read-through**: the cache library loads from the database on a miss. **Write-through**: each write updates the cache and the database synchronously, so the cache stays warm but writes are slower. **Write-behind**: write to the cache and flush to the database later, which is fast but loses data if the cache dies first. Evict with LRU, LFU or TTLs, and always set a TTL, so an invalidation bug cannot leave data stale forever.

Invalidation is where caches go wrong. A race in cache-aside: a reader misses and reads v1 from the database; a writer updates the database to v2 and deletes the cache key; the reader then stores v1, and it stays stale until the TTL expires. Facebook's memcache solves this with **leases**: a miss returns a token, a delete invalidates outstanding tokens, and a set with an invalidated token is rejected. On writes, delete the key rather than setting it. A **stampede** happens when a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database together; prevent it with request coalescing (single-flight), leases, or refreshing the value just before it expires.

points: Read: cache → on miss, DB → fill cache
Write: update DB, then delete the cache key
Only requested data is cached
First read after a write or expiry is a miss
Race: a slow reader can store a stale value

example.explain: An OrderedDict keeps keys in recency order: `move_to_end` marks a key as just used and `popitem(last=False)` removes the oldest. Both operations are O(1), which is how real LRU caches work (a hash map plus a doubly linked list).

Read-through
Write-through
Write-behind (write-back)
questions.explain: Write-behind acknowledges once the cache has the write and flushes to the database later, so a crash loses whatever has not been flushed. In the other three patterns the database holds every acknowledged write, so losing the cache only costs performance.

questions.prompt: The home page's data is cached under one key with a 60 s TTL. Every minute, right when it expires, database CPU hits 100% and p99 latency spikes. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Lower the TTL to 10 s
Coalesce misses so one request recomputes the value while the others wait or get the stale copy (single-flight or a lease), or refresh it shortly before expiry
Add more database replicas
Switch the eviction policy from LRU to LFU
questions.explain: This is a stampede: thousands of concurrent misses on one key at the same instant. Coalescing makes it a single query. A shorter TTL makes stampedes six times more frequent; replicas only raise how big a stampede you can survive; the eviction policy is irrelevant, because the key expired rather than being evicted.

questions.prompt: With cache-aside, a slow reader misses, reads v1 from the database, and stalls. Meanwhile a writer updates the database to v2 and deletes the cache key. The reader then sets the cache to v1. Which change closes this race?
options: Write the new value into the cache before updating the database
Leases: a miss hands the reader a token, the writer's delete invalidates it, and the reader's late set is rejected
Increase the TTL
Use LFU instead of LRU
questions.explain: The problem is a set based on a read older than the latest invalidation. Leases (Facebook's memcache design) reject exactly those sets. Writing the cache before the database leaves the cache wrong if the database write fails, and a longer TTL makes the stale value live longer.

video.title: Caching Strategies Explained: Cache-Aside, Write-Through & Write-Back

lessons.why: Caches make systems fast and cheap, and stale or stampeding caches cause some of the most confusing outages. Choosing the pattern and invalidation strategy matters.

terms.d: App reads cache, on a miss reads the database and fills the cache.
Write cache and database together / write cache now, database later.
hit rate × cache latency + miss rate × database latency.
Many clients missing at once and hammering the database; prevented with leases or locks.

mistakes.wrong: Deleting the cache key after a write prevents stale data.
mistakes.right: A concurrent reader can put an old value back. Use leases, versions or short TTLs.

mistakes.wrong: A 90% hit rate means 90% less latency.
mistakes.right: Misses dominate: 0.9 × 1 ms + 0.1 × 50 ms is still 5.9 ms.

takeaways: Cache-aside is the default; know its races.
Compute effective latency from the hit rate.
Protect against stampedes with leases, request coalescing or jittered TTLs.

lessons.title: Load balancing
lessons.objective: By the end you can compare L4 and L7 load balancers and the round-robin, least-connections and power-of-two-choices algorithms, and configure health checks that do not cause a cascading failure.
concept: A load balancer spreads requests across a pool of backends and stops sending to unhealthy ones. An **L4** balancer (AWS NLB, LVS, Google's Maglev) forwards TCP or UDP connections by their address and port tuple without parsing the payload: very fast, but one long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connection carries every request to the same backend. An **L7** balancer (nginx, Envoy, HAProxy, AWS ALB) terminates TLS, parses HTTP, routes by path or header, and balances per request, at the cost of more CPU. DNS-based balancing is coarse, because clients cache records, sometimes beyond their TTL.

Algorithms: **round robin** is fine when requests and backends are uniform. **Least connections** (or least outstanding requests) adapts to slow backends. **Power of two choices** picks two backends at random and sends to the less loaded one. It gets nearly the balance of always choosing the least-loaded backend, without global state, and it avoids **herding**, where many balancers with the same stale view all pick the same 'emptiest' backend. **Consistent hashing** gives affinity (cache locality, sessions); bounded-load variants cap how much one backend can receive.

Health checks come in two kinds: active (probe `/healthz` every few seconds) and passive (outlier detection: eject a backend after, say, 5 consecutive 5xx responses). The trap: a health check that also tests a shared dependency, such as the database, makes every backend fail at once when that dependency blips, and the balancer removes the whole pool, causing a total outage. Keep liveness checks shallow, use a panic threshold (Envoy, for example, ignores health status when too many hosts look unhealthy), and slow-start new instances so cold caches are not hit with a full share of traffic.

left.title: L4 (transport)
points: Balances connections by IP/port tuple
No TLS termination or HTTP parsing; very high throughput
One HTTP/2 connection = one backend for all its requests
Examples: AWS NLB, LVS, Maglev

right.title: L7 (application)
points: Balances individual HTTP/gRPC requests
Routes by path, header or cookie; can retry and rewrite
Costs CPU for TLS and parsing
Examples: Envoy, nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB

example.code:
import random

rng = random.Random(7)
n, m = 100, 100_000                # 100 backends, 100,000 requests (no departures)
rand_load, p2c_load = [0] * n, [0] * n
for _ in range(m):
    rand_load[rng.randrange(n)] += 1
    a, b = rng.randrange(n), rng.randrange(n)
    p2c_load[a if p2c_load[a] <= p2c_load[b] else b] += 1
print("mean", m // n, "max random", max(rand_load), "max p2c", max(p2c_load))
example.explain: With purely random choice the busiest backend ends up noticeably above the mean of 1,000, while two random choices keep the maximum within a couple of requests of it. Sampling just one extra backend gives an exponential improvement in the worst case.

lessons.tryit: Extend the example into a time-based simulation: requests arrive every 1 ms, 10 backends each take an exponential service time with a mean of 8 ms, and one backend is 5× slower. Compare round robin, random, least connections and power of two choices on p99 latency. Then give all four algorithms a view of backend load that is 50 ms stale and report which one degrades most and why.

options: Spreading TCP connections across backends
Routing /api/* and /static/* to different pools
Removing a backend that refuses connections
Handling millions of packets per second
questions.explain: Path-based routing needs the HTTP request parsed, which happens at L7. L4 balancers distribute connections, can health-check by connecting, and are usually the faster option.

questions.prompt: A least-connections balancer assigns 4 new requests. Ties go to the first backend in dict order. What does this print?

active = {"a": 2, "b": 0, "c": 1}
order = []
for _ in range(4):
    pick = min(active, key=active.get)
    active[pick] += 1
    order.append(pick)
print("".join(order))
questions.explain: b (0) gets the first request → b=1. Now a=2, b=1, c=1: the tie between b and c goes to b, the first in dict order → b=2. Now c=1 is the minimum → c=2. Finally all are 2, so a wins the tie. Answering 'bcab' forgets that b is still tied for least after its first request.

questions.prompt: Each backend's /healthz returns 200 only if it can run `SELECT 1` on the shared database. The database has a 20-second failover. What happens, and what is the better design?
options: Only the backends that cannot reach the database are removed
Every backend fails its health check at once, the balancer removes the whole pool, and even requests that don't need the database fail; keep /healthz shallow and handle database errors per request
Nothing, because health checks are only advisory
The balancer sends traffic to the database directly
questions.explain: A deep health check turns a shared dependency's blip into a total outage: when every backend is 'unhealthy', the balancer has nowhere to send traffic. A shallow liveness check plus per-request degradation (cached data, error pages for database-dependent paths) keeps the rest of the site up. A panic threshold is the safety net.

questions.prompt: Three independent load balancers use least-connections with load information that is refreshed every second. A new backend joins with 0 connections, and within a second it is overloaded while the others are fine. Why, and what helps?
options: The new backend is faulty
Herding: all three balancers see the same stale 'least loaded' backend and pile onto it; power of two choices (or least connections with slow start) spreads the load
Round robin would have been worse
Least connections never works with more than one balancer
questions.explain: With a stale shared view, 'pick the minimum' sends everything to the same target until the next refresh. Randomized two-choice selection is resistant to stale information, and slow start ramps a new instance up gradually. Round robin would in fact have avoided this particular pile-up, and least connections works with several balancers when its information is fresh.

Send to the backend with the fewest outstanding requests.
Pick two random backends, send to the less loaded.
Active probes or passive outlier detection to remove bad backends.

mistakes.wrong: Round robin is always fair.
mistakes.right: With uneven requests or a slow backend it piles work onto the struggling one.

mistakes.right: Then one shared dependency failing ejects every backend at once. Check what the instance itself controls.

lessons.title: Tail latency: why p99 dominates at scale
lessons.objective: By the end you can compute how fan-out turns a rare slow backend into a common slow request, measure percentiles correctly, and apply hedging, deadlines and isolation to cut p99.
concept: Averages hide pain, so report percentiles: p50 (the median), p99 (1 request in 100 is slower) and p99.9. Fan-out makes the tail common. A page that calls 100 backends in parallel is as slow as the slowest one. If each backend is slow 1% of the time, the page is slow with probability 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 63%. Dean and Barroso's 'The Tail at Scale' (2013) makes the point: at scale, the tail latency of the components becomes the typical latency of the system.

Tail latency comes from GC pauses, background compaction, noisy neighbours on shared hardware, bursts of queueing, TCP retransmission timeouts (at least 200 ms on Linux by default), cold caches and lock contention. You cannot remove all of them, so you design to tolerate them. Measure carefully: percentiles do not average (the mean of 20 hosts' p99 values is not the fleet's p99), so merge histograms (HdrHistogram, t-digest). Beware **coordinated omission**: a load generator that waits for each response before sending the next one stops sending exactly when the server stalls, so it under-reports the tail.

Techniques from the paper. **Hedged requests**: if a reply hasn't arrived by about the p95 latency, send the same request to another replica and use whichever answer comes first. In Google's BigTable benchmark, a 10 ms hedge cut p99.9 latency for a 1,000-key read from 1,800 ms to 74 ms with only 2% more requests. **Tied requests** go to two replicas, and the first to start cancels the other. Also: set deadlines on every call, split data into many small partitions so a slow one is cheap to move, throttle background work such as compaction, and keep queues bounded.

visual.title: Chance a request touches at least one slow call (each call slow 1% of the time)

example.code:
import math

def percentile(samples, p):
    s = sorted(samples)
    k = math.ceil(p / 100 * len(s)) - 1   # nearest-rank method
    return s[max(k, 0)]

lat_ms = [12, 15, 11, 14, 13, 12, 16, 15, 13, 900]
print(sum(lat_ms) / len(lat_ms), percentile(lat_ms, 50), percentile(lat_ms, 99))
example.explain: Nearest-rank takes the value at position ceil(p% × n) in sorted order. One 900 ms outlier drags the mean to 102.1 ms, a latency no request actually had, while the median of 13 ms describes the typical request and the p99 of 900 ms shows the tail.

Then add hedging: if a call hasn't returned by 15 ms, send a second copy (with an independent latency) and take the faster; report the new p50/p99 and the percentage of extra calls. Finally, compute the 'average of p99s' across 10 simulated hosts and compare it with the true merged p99.

99% of requests complete in 250 ms or less, and 1% take longer
The slowest request took 250 ms
99 requests per second take 250 ms

import math

def percentile(samples, p):
    s = sorted(samples)
    k = math.ceil(p / 100 * len(s)) - 1
    return s[max(k, 0)]

lat_ms = [12, 15, 11, 14, 13, 12, 16, 15, 13, 900]

questions.prompt: A search request fans out to 100 leaf servers. Leaf latency is p50 = 10 ms, p95 = 25 ms, p99 = 300 ms. You add hedged requests. After how long should a leaf request be hedged?

After about the p95 (≈25 ms), so roughly 5% of requests get a second copy
After the p99 (300 ms)
Never; raise the overall timeout instead
questions.explain: Hedging at around p95 caps the extra load at about 5% and cuts off the slow tail. Sending every request twice doubles the load and can create the very slowness you are fighting; hedging only after 300 ms leaves the whole tail in place.

questions.prompt: A dashboard computes 'fleet p99' as the average of the p99 values of 20 hosts and shows 120 ms. Users report many slow requests, and one host has a p99 of 2 s while handling 30% of the traffic. What is wrong, and how should fleet p99 be computed?
options: Nothing; averaging percentiles is standard
Percentiles cannot be averaged, especially across hosts with different traffic; merge the hosts' latency histograms and take the p99 of the combined distribution
Use the median of the hosts' p99 values instead
Take the maximum of the hosts' p99 values
questions.explain: The fleet percentile depends on the full distribution and on how much traffic each host serves; an average or median of per-host percentiles ignores both. The maximum is a pessimistic bound, not the fleet p99. Mergeable histograms such as HdrHistogram or t-digest give the right number.

mistakes.right: Averages hide the slow tail. Track p99 and p99.9.

project.title: Rate limiter + caching proxy, load-tested to p99
project.brief: Build an HTTP reverse proxy (Go recommended) in front of a deliberately slow origin server, with per-client token-bucket rate limiting, a TTL'd LRU cache with single-flight, bounded queues with load shedding, and hedged requests. Load-test every stage with an open-loop generator and report p50, p99 and p99.9, so every optimization is backed by a measured number.
milestones: Origin and pass-through: write an origin with random 20–200 ms latency, where 1% of requests take 2 s; put a pass-through proxy (httputil.ReverseProxy) in front of it; measure a baseline with an open-loop generator (for example `vegeta attack -rate=500/s`) to avoid coordinated omission.
Rate limiter: a token bucket per API key (50 req/s, burst 100) returning 429 with Retry-After; prove with a test that a client sending 200 req/s gets about 50 req/s through.
Cache: an LRU with TTL and a size bound for GET responses, plus single-flight so a cold hot key causes exactly one origin request; report the hit rate and the new latency percentiles.
Overload behaviour: bound the in-flight request queue and shed with 503 when it is full; propagate a 1 s deadline to the origin; compare latency and goodput at 2× capacity with and without shedding.
Hedging: run two origin replicas and hedge after the measured p95; write a one-page report with latency histograms for every stage and the extra load hedging cost.
project.stretch: Share the rate limiter across 3 proxy instances through Redis (an atomic Lua script implementing the token bucket), and measure the added per-request latency and how far the enforced rate drifts under a network partition between a proxy and Redis.

exam.prompt: Token bucket with rate 2 tokens/s and capacity 3, starting full at t=0. What does this print?
exam.answer: [True, True, True, False, True, False, True]
exam.explain: The burst of 3 passes and the fourth request at t=0 finds 0 tokens. At t=0.5 one token has refilled (0.5 s × 2/s), and it is spent. At t=0.6 only 0.2 tokens exist, so the request is refused. At t=2.0, 1.4 s × 2 = 2.8 more tokens bring the bucket to 3.0, so the last request passes. The bucket refills continuously, not one token per whole second.

exam.prompt: An asyncio service calls the synchronous `requests.get()` to fetch cache misses from an origin that takes 200 ms. At 50 requests/s with a 20% miss rate, p99 latency is terrible even for cache hits. Why?
options: The cache hit rate is too low
Each synchronous call blocks the event loop for 200 ms, so cache hits queue behind misses; use an async HTTP client or run the call in an executor
asyncio cannot handle 50 requests/s
The origin needs more replicas
exam.explain: 10 misses/s × 200 ms means the loop is blocked about 2 seconds out of every second, which is impossible to sustain, so everything queues. Hits are cheap, but they need the loop to run. An async client lets the loop serve hits while misses wait on the network.

exam.prompt: During an overload, a thread-per-request server receives 300 requests/s, and its latency has grown to 2 s. By Little's law, about how many threads are busy?
exam.explain: L = λW = 300/s × 2 s = 600. When latency grows under overload, the number of requests in flight grows with it, which is how thread pools and connection pools run out. Bounding concurrency and shedding the excess keeps W from growing.

exam.prompt: A hot cache key expires, a stampede overloads the database, requests pile up in the app servers' queues, and clients' immediate retries (module 1) double the load. Which combination breaks this cycle most directly?
options: Increase the database's connection limit
Single-flight on cache misses, bounded queues with load shedding, and client retries with exponential backoff, jitter and a retry budget
Add a second cache layer with the same TTL
Remove TTLs so keys never expire
exam.explain: Each part removes one amplifier: coalescing turns N misses into 1 query, bounded queues stop latency (and in-flight work) from growing without limit, and backoff with a budget stops retries from multiplying the load. More connections let more load reach the already overloaded database; removing TTLs leaves data stale forever after an invalidation bug.

exam.prompt: A client library caches reads from your linearizable Raft-backed KV store (module 3) for 5 seconds. What guarantee do clients lose?
options: Durability
Linearizability: a read can return a value up to 5 seconds old even after a newer write has completed
Nothing, because Raft guarantees freshness
Availability
exam.explain: The store is still linearizable, but reads served from a client cache bypass it, so a read that starts after a completed write can return the older value. Durability is unchanged, since writes still go through Raft. If anything, availability improves, because cached reads keep working while the store is unreachable.

exam.prompt: Each of 100 parallel calls is slow 0.1% of the time. What fraction of requests hit at least one slow call?
exam.explain: 0.999¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.9048, so about 9.5% of requests are slow, even though each backend is slow only 0.1% of the time: fan-out multiplies the tail by roughly the fan-out factor while the probability is small. The tempting answer 0.001 ignores the fan-out.

exam.prompt: gRPC clients connect through an L4 load balancer to 10 backends. After a deploy, one backend runs at 90% CPU while the others are at 10%. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The busy backend has a memory leak; restart it
gRPC multiplexes many requests over a few long-lived HTTP/2 connections, and L4 balances connections, not requests; use an L7 (gRPC-aware) balancer or client-side balancing, and cap connection age
The L4 balancer is using round robin
TCP keepalives are disabled
exam.explain: After the deploy, clients reconnected and most of their long-lived connections happened to land on one backend; every request on a connection follows it. Per-request (L7) balancing fixes the imbalance, and a maximum connection age makes clients reconnect and rebalance over time. Round robin over connections is the same problem, not its cause.

modules.title: System design practice
modules.summary: A repeatable method for turning vague requirements into a defended design: estimates first, then the URL shortener and chat/feed classics, then the SLOs, alerts and reliability practices that keep it running.

lessons.title: Requirements to design: a method and back-of-envelope estimates
lessons.objective: By the end you can run a six-step design method and produce QPS, storage and bandwidth estimates, accurate to within about 2×, in under five minutes.
concept: A design that holds up under questioning follows the same six steps. (1) **Requirements**: functional (what users do) and non-functional (scale, latency targets, availability, consistency, durability); ask instead of assuming. (2) **Estimates**: average and peak QPS, storage per year, bandwidth, cache memory. (3) **API**: a handful of endpoints. (4) **Data model** and storage choice. (5) **High-level diagram**. (6) **Deep dives** into the bottleneck the estimates revealed, and into failure modes. Every box on the diagram should trace back to a requirement or a number.

Numbers to memorize. A day is 86,400 s, roughly 10⁵, so 1 million requests a day is about 12 per second; peak is usually 2–3× the average. Main memory reference: ~100 ns. SSD random read: ~100 µs. Round trip within a datacenter: ~0.5 ms. Disk seek: ~10 ms. California to the Netherlands and back: ~150 ms. A well-tuned single Postgres server handles thousands to tens of thousands of simple queries per second; a single Redis node, on the order of 100,000 simple operations per second.

Estimation is about orders of magnitude, so round hard and say your assumptions out loud: 100M daily users × 10 reads a day = 10⁹ reads/day ≈ 10⁴ QPS average, 3 × 10⁴ peak. Then let the numbers drive the design. 30,000 read QPS means you need a cache tier. 1 KB × 10⁸ writes/day = 100 GB/day ≈ 36 TB/year, which means sharding. 10,000 QPS × 10 KB responses = 100 MB/s ≈ 800 Mbit/s of egress. Write the estimate table first; it is what you will defend every later choice with.

visual.title: Latency numbers to keep in your head (approximate)

example.code:
DAU = 100e6
reads_per_user, writes_per_user = 20, 2
avg_read_qps = DAU * reads_per_user / 86_400
peak_read_qps = 3 * avg_read_qps
storage_tb_per_year = DAU * writes_per_user * 1_000 * 365 / 1e12   # 1 KB per write
print(f"avg reads {avg_read_qps:,.0f}/s  peak {peak_read_qps:,.0f}/s  storage {storage_tb_per_year:.0f} TB/yr")
example.explain: Prints `avg reads 23,148/s  peak 69,444/s  storage 73 TB/yr`. In an interview you would say 'about 25k average, 70k peak, about 75 TB a year', then conclude that you need a cache tier for reads and a sharded store for writes.

lessons.tryit: Without looking anything up, estimate for a photo-sharing app with 50M DAU, where each user views 30 photos and uploads 0.5 photos a day (average 2 MB, plus a 50 KB thumbnail): average and peak read QPS, upload QPS, storage per year with 3× replication, and egress bandwidth if 80% of views are served by a CDN. Then check your arithmetic in Python and write down the two design decisions the numbers force.

questions.prompt: For quick estimates, roughly how many seconds are in a day?
options: About 10³
About 10⁴
About 10⁵
About 10⁶
questions.explain: 86,400 ≈ 10⁵ (8.64 × 10⁴). This one number turns 'per day' into 'per second': divide by about 100,000. Using 10⁴ inflates every QPS estimate tenfold.

questions.prompt: 50M daily users each make 4 requests per day. What is the average QPS?
questions.code: print(round(50e6 * 4 / 86_400))
questions.explain: 2 × 10⁸ requests ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 2,314.8, which rounds to 2,315. The mental shortcut 2 × 10⁸ ÷ 10⁵ = 2,000 is within 15%, close enough for design decisions; peak would be around 5,000–7,000.

questions.prompt: Your estimate shows 5,000 writes/s of 2 KB each, kept forever with 3× replication. What does that imply?
options: A single Postgres server with a big disk is fine for years
About 10 MB/s, ~860 GB/day, ~315 TB/year raw and ~1 PB/year replicated: you need a horizontally partitioned store (or object storage) and a retention/tiering plan from day one
Writes this small can live in a Redis cache
Storage does not matter; only QPS does
questions.explain: 5,000 × 2 KB = 10 MB/s; × 86,400 ≈ 864 GB/day; × 365 ≈ 315 TB/year; × 3 ≈ 0.95 PB/year. No single server holds that, and RAM certainly does not. The QPS on its own looks modest, which is exactly why you have to compute storage too.

questions.prompt: Midway through a design review, you are asked: 'Why Cassandra for the timeline store?' Which answer is the strongest defense?
options: Because Netflix and Apple use it

Because our estimate is 70,000 writes/s at peak and 73 TB/year of append-only data accessed by user_id; a partitioned wide-column store with user_id as the partition key scales writes horizontally, and our requirements accept eventual consistency for timelines
Because NoSQL is faster than SQL
Because it is the most popular database for big data
questions.explain: A defense connects the choice to measured requirements (write rate, data size, access pattern, acceptable consistency). Popularity and 'NoSQL is faster' are not reasons; a reviewer will ask 'faster at what, for which access pattern?'

lessons.title: Designing a URL shortener
lessons.objective: By the end you can produce a complete URL-shortener design (estimates, API, ID generation, storage, caching, redirects) and defend your choices of 301 vs 302 and of ID scheme.
concept: Requirements: create a short link for a long URL; redirect; optionally custom aliases and expiry; click analytics. Non-functional: redirects must be fast and highly available, and codes must never collide. Assume 100M new links a month with a 100:1 read-to-write ratio: writes ≈ 100M ÷ (30 × 86,400) ≈ 40/s, reads ≈ 4,000/s on average and perhaps 10,000/s at peak. Storage: 500 bytes per link × 100M × 12 months × 5 years = 3 TB. This is a read-heavy system with small data, which makes it easy to cache.

IDs use **base62** (0–9, a–z, A–Z): 7 characters give 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 × 10¹² codes, enough for thousands of years at 1.2 billion links a year. Options: (a) **hash** the long URL (MD5) and keep 7 characters: the same URL always gets the same code, but collisions must be detected and resolved. (b) **Counter + base62**: unique and short, but the codes are sequential (guessable) and one counter is a bottleneck; fix that by leasing blocks of 1,000 IDs to each app server. (c) **Random** 7 characters inserted under a unique constraint, retrying on the rare conflict.

Storage is a key/value lookup by code, so any KV store or Postgres with a primary key works; 3 TB fits on a few shards. Popularity follows a power law, so cache hot codes in Redis or at a CDN edge. For the redirect, **301 (permanent)** lets browsers cache it, so less load reaches you, but you lose click counts and can never change the target; **302 or 307** brings every click to you. Send click events asynchronously to a log such as Kafka, never on the redirect's critical path. Against abuse, rate-limit link creation and scan target URLs for malware.

steps.detail: Browser hits the edge or load balancer

steps.label: Cache lookup
steps.detail: Redis: code → long URL (high hit rate)

steps.label: On miss: DB
steps.detail: Primary-key lookup, then fill the cache

steps.label: 302 Location
steps.detail: Browser follows the long URL

steps.label: Async click event
steps.detail: Kafka → analytics, off the critical path

example.explain: Repeated divmod by 62 produces the digits from least significant up, so they are reversed at the end. 125 = 2 × 62 + 1 encodes as '21', and the largest 7-character code, 62⁷ − 1, is 'ZZZZZZZ'.

lessons.tryit: Write a one-page design for the URL shortener using the method from the last lesson: requirements, an estimate table, three API endpoints, the schema, a diagram, and two deep dives (ID generation and caching). Then implement the core in about 100 lines: a Flask or FastAPI app with SQLite, block-leased counter IDs encoded in base62, 302 redirects and an in-process LRU cache, and load-test redirects to report their p99.

questions.prompt: The business wants accurate click counts for every short link. Which redirect status should the service return?
options: 301 Moved Permanently
302 Found (or 307)
200 with a JavaScript redirect
404, so the browser retries
questions.explain: Browsers may cache a 301 and go straight to the target on later clicks, so those clicks never reach you. A 302 or 307 is not cached by default, so every click is counted. A JavaScript redirect adds a full page load and breaks clients that do not run scripts.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: 3843 = 62² − 1 = 61 × 62 + 61, and digit 61 is 'Z', so the code is 'ZZ', the largest 2-character code. A common slip is to forget the reverse; here both digits are the same, so the result would hide that bug, which is why you should also test a value such as 125 → '21'.

questions.prompt: Your shortener uses a global counter with base62, so codes come out as …aZ3k, …aZ3l, …aZ3m. A competitor scrapes every link (including 'unlisted' shared documents) by incrementing codes. What is the best fix?
options: Add a CAPTCHA to the redirect

Make codes non-sequential: random IDs under a unique constraint, or a reversible permutation of the counter (for example a keyed Feistel network over the ID space), and use longer codes for private links
Switch from base62 to base64
Rate-limit link creation
questions.explain: The leak comes from predictability. Random or permuted IDs make the code space sparse, so guessing becomes impractical, especially with longer codes. A CAPTCHA on redirects breaks every legitimate click; base64 is just as sequential; limiting creation does nothing to stop someone reading links.

questions.prompt: You generate codes by taking the first 7 base62 characters of MD5(long_url), giving about 3.5 × 10¹² possible codes. Roughly how many links can you store before a collision between two different URLs becomes likely?
options: About 3.5 × 10¹², because every code is used once
About 2 million, by the birthday bound √N ≈ 1.9 × 10⁶, so collision detection and resolution are required
About 1 billion
Never, because MD5 has no collisions on 7 characters
questions.explain: By the birthday paradox, collisions become likely after about √N items, and √(3.5 × 10¹²) ≈ 1.9 million: a few days of traffic at 100M links a month. Truncating any hash function means you must check for a collision on insert and, for example, re-hash with a salt.

mistakes.right: Browsers cache it, so you lose click analytics and can't change the target. Use 302 or 307 if you need them.
