lessons.title: Designing a chat and news-feed system
lessons.objective: By the end you can design a chat service (delivery, ordering, offline sync) and a news feed, and use estimates to justify a hybrid fan-out strategy.
concept: Chat requirements: one-to-one and group messages, in order within each conversation, delivered to offline users later, with read receipts and presence. Clients keep a persistent **WebSocket** to a gateway server; an epoll-based gateway can hold 100,000 or more mostly idle connections, and a session service maps each user to their gateway. Sending: client → gateway → chat service, which assigns the next **per-conversation sequence number** and persists the message (for example in Cassandra, partitioned by conversation_id and ordered by seq) before acknowledging. It then pushes to the recipients' gateways. Offline users get a push notification and, on reconnect, fetch everything after their last seen seq. A client-generated message ID makes retries idempotent.

A news feed (home timeline) merges recent posts from everyone you follow, newest first. **Fan-out on read (pull)**: at read time, fetch each followee's recent posts and merge them; writes are cheap and reads are expensive. **Fan-out on write (push)**: when someone posts, insert the post ID into each follower's precomputed timeline (for example a capped Redis list); reads become a single lookup, but a celebrity with 50M followers turns one post into 50M writes. Since people read far more often than they post, push is the usual default.

Hence the **hybrid**: push for ordinary accounts; for accounts above a follower threshold (say 1M), skip the fan-out and merge their recent posts at read time. Twitter described essentially this design. Check it with estimates: 200M DAU loading their timeline 10 times a day is 2 × 10⁹ ÷ 86,400 ≈ 23,000 read QPS. One post per user per day with 200 followers on average is 4 × 10¹⁰ timeline inserts a day ≈ 460,000 writes/s, feasible on a Redis cluster because each entry is only an 8-byte post ID. Timelines store IDs only; post bodies come from a separate post cache.

points: On post: insert the ID into every follower's timeline
Read = one list lookup, very fast
Celebrity post = millions of writes and delivery lag
Wasted work for inactive followers

Read = fetch every followee's posts and merge

example.explain: The hybrid read path: one Redis read for the precomputed part, plus a few celebrity lists merged on the fly. `heapq.merge` combines already-sorted lists lazily, so taking the top 20 costs O(20 × log of the number of lists), not a full sort.

lessons.tryit: Draw the chat design end to end: client, gateways, session service, chat service, message store and push service. Trace three scenarios on it: a group message to five members, two of them offline; a gateway crash with 100,000 connected users; and the same message retried by a client after a timeout. For each, write which component guarantees ordering, durability and no duplicates.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of pure fan-out on write for a news feed?
options: Reads are slow
Accounts with millions of followers turn each post into millions of timeline writes, delaying delivery
Posts cannot be deleted
It requires strong consistency
questions.explain: Push makes reads cheap by doing the work at write time, and that work grows with the number of followers. Slow reads are the weakness of pull, not push; deletions and consistency are manageable in either design.

questions.prompt: With a hybrid fan-out that skips authors above 1M followers, how many timeline writes do these three posts cause?
questions.explain: Alice and Bob are pushed (300 + 150 timeline writes); the celebrity is skipped and merged at read time. Without the threshold the total would be 40,000,450 writes for three posts, which is exactly the problem the hybrid solves.

questions.prompt: Two members of a group chat send messages at the same moment through different gateway servers, and each message is ordered by its gateway's wall-clock timestamp. Different recipients see the two messages in different orders, and sometimes a reply appears before the message it answers. What is the fix?
options: Synchronize the gateways' clocks with NTP more often
Have one owner per conversation (for example the leader of its partition) assign increasing sequence numbers, and have clients display messages in seq order
Sort by the sender's device clock instead
Use vector clocks and show concurrent messages side by side
questions.explain: Wall clocks drift and jump (module 1), and better NTP only shrinks the error. A single sequencer per conversation gives every client the same total order, and a reply always gets a higher seq than the message the sender saw. Device clocks are worse still, and vector clocks would only detect the concurrency, not decide one order for everybody.

questions.prompt: A chat gateway holding 100,000 WebSocket connections crashes. What design keeps users from losing messages or overwhelming the remaining gateways?
options: Store undelivered messages in the gateway's memory and restore them after a restart
Persist every message before acknowledging it; clients reconnect to other gateways with jittered backoff and fetch every message after their last seen seq
Have every client reconnect immediately so downtime is minimal
Make each gateway replicate its connections to a standby
questions.explain: Gateways should be stateless: the message store is the source of truth, so a crash loses connections, not messages. Jitter spreads 100,000 reconnects out over time instead of a thundering herd, and the seq cursor makes catching up exact. Gateway memory dies with the crash, and live TCP connections cannot be replicated to a standby.

lessons.title: Observability, SLOs and error budgets
lessons.objective: By the end you can define SLIs and an SLO for a service, compute its error budget, and design a burn-rate alert that pages on user pain rather than on CPU usage.
concept: A system is observable when you can answer new questions about production without shipping new code. There are three kinds of signal. **Metrics** are cheap aggregated counters and histograms: rate, errors and duration (RED) for services, or utilization, saturation and errors (USE) for resources. **Logs** are structured events, and expensive at high volume. **Traces** follow one request across services as a tree of spans (OpenTelemetry), joined by a propagated trace ID. Record latency as histograms, not averages, and watch label cardinality: a label holding user IDs creates millions of time series.

An **SLI** (service level indicator) is a measured ratio of good events, for example the fraction of HTTP requests that return a non-5xx response in under 300 ms. An **SLO** is a target for it over a window: 99.9% over 30 days. An **SLA** is a contract with penalties, deliberately looser than the SLO. The **error budget** is 1 − SLO: 0.1% of 30 days is 43.2 minutes of total downtime, or 0.1% of requests failing. While budget remains, ship features quickly; when it runs out, freeze risky launches and fix reliability. That turns the reliability-versus-velocity argument into arithmetic.

Page on symptoms (users are hurting), not on causes (CPU at 90%). The **burn rate** is the observed error rate divided by the budgeted rate (0.1% here). At burn rate 1 you spend exactly the whole budget in 30 days; at burn rate 14.4 you spend 2% of the monthly budget in one hour. The Google SRE Workbook recommends multi-window alerts: page when the burn rate exceeds 14.4 over 1 hour (confirmed over the last 5 minutes) or 6 over 6 hours, and open a ticket when it exceeds 1 over 3 days. Every page must be something a human can act on.

example.code:
slo = 0.999
budget = 1 - slo                                # 0.1% of requests may fail
window_requests, window_errors = 120_000, 840   # the last hour
error_rate = window_errors / window_requests    # 0.7%
burn_rate = error_rate / budget
print(f"burn rate {burn_rate:.1f}; budget spent this hour {burn_rate / 720:.1%}")
example.explain: A 0.7% error rate against a 0.1% budget is a burn rate of 7: this hour used 7/720 of the month's budget (720 hours in 30 days), about 1%. That is above the 6× six-hour paging threshold if it persists, but below the 14.4× fast-burn threshold.

lessons.tryit: For a service you know (or the URL shortener from s6m5l2), write two SLIs with exact definitions (what counts as good, where it is measured), an SLO for each, and the error budget in both minutes and requests at 50M requests/month. Then write the Prometheus-style alert expressions (or pseudocode) for the 14.4×/1 h and 6×/6 h burn-rate pages, and a one-paragraph error-budget policy that says what happens when the budget is exhausted.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an SLO and an SLA?
options: They are the same thing
An SLO is an internal reliability target; an SLA is an external contract with consequences, usually set looser than the SLO
An SLA is measured and an SLO is not
An SLO applies to latency and an SLA to availability
questions.explain: You want to notice and fix problems while you are still inside your SLA, so the internal SLO is stricter. Both can cover any SLI (latency, availability, freshness), and both must be measured.

questions.prompt: How many minutes of full downtime does a 99.95% SLO allow in 30 days?
questions.explain: 30 days = 43,200 minutes, and 0.05% of that is 21.6 minutes (the floating-point result 21.600000000000016 rounds to 21.6). Half of a 99.9% budget (43.2 minutes); each extra nine divides the budget by ten.

questions.prompt: A team pages on CPU > 80%. Nightly batch jobs page them with no user impact, yet a bad config that made 3% of requests fail at normal CPU went unnoticed for two hours. What should replace the CPU alert?
options: Raise the CPU threshold to 95%
SLO burn-rate alerts on the user-facing error-rate SLI (for example a page at 14.4× over 1 h, confirmed over 5 min), with CPU kept on a dashboard
Page on every 5xx response
Add a memory alert alongside the CPU alert
questions.explain: A 3% error rate against a 0.1% budget is a 30× burn, which a burn-rate alert pages on within minutes, while the batch jobs never trip it because users are not affected. A higher CPU threshold still misses config bugs; paging on every 5xx is noise; a memory alert is just another cause-based alert.

questions.prompt: The team's agreed policy says an exhausted error budget freezes non-critical launches. After a bad outage, the 30-day budget for a 99.9% SLO is gone in week 2, and product wants to launch a big feature this week. What does the policy imply?
options: Launch anyway; budgets are only advisory
Hold the launch and put engineering time into reliability fixes until the rolling budget is positive again (or until the exception process the policy defines is used)
Lower the SLO to 99% so the budget is positive again
Stop measuring the SLI until next month
questions.explain: An error budget only works if the agreed consequence actually happens; otherwise the SLO is decoration. Quietly lowering the SLO or pausing measurement cheats the arithmetic. If the business really needs the launch, it goes through the policy's documented exception path, not around it.

A target for an SLI over a window, like 99.9% over 30 days.

Error budget = 1 − SLO.

lessons.title: Reliability: redundancy, graceful degradation, postmortems
lessons.objective: By the end you can compute availability for components in series and in parallel, design degraded modes for a failing dependency, and write a blameless postmortem with useful action items.
concept: Availability math: components a request needs **in series** multiply. A path through a load balancer (99.99%), an app (99.9%) and a database (99.9%) gets about 99.79%. Redundant components **in parallel** (any one is enough) fail only if all fail: two independent 99% replicas give 1 − 0.01² = 99.99%. The catch is the word independent. Shared power, a bad config pushed everywhere at once, a common software bug or a whole region failing make failures correlated, and the biggest outages are usually correlated, often triggered by a change. So place replicas across failure domains (racks, availability zones, regions), roll changes out in stages, and keep rollback fast.

**Graceful degradation** means deciding in advance what to serve when a dependency fails. Recommendations down? Show a static bestseller list. Personalization times out after 50 ms? Render the generic page. Search index stale? Serve it with a banner. The tools: timeouts; **circuit breakers** (after N consecutive failures, stop calling for a cool-off period and fail fast, then let one probe through); **bulkheads** (separate thread or connection pools, so one slow dependency cannot use up every thread); priority-based load shedding; and feature flags as kill switches. Verify them with fault injection: game days and chaos experiments.

After an incident, write a **blameless postmortem**: a summary, the impact (users affected, duration, error budget consumed), a timeline, the root causes and contributing factors, what went well and badly, and action items with owners and due dates. Blameless means assuming people made reasonable decisions with the information and tools they had, so the fix goes into the system (guardrails, automation, alerts, safer defaults), not into 'be more careful'. Track the action items to completion: the value of a postmortem is in the changes it leads to.

items.label: Timeout
items.detail: Bound how long any one call can hold a thread

items.label: Retry with budget
items.detail: Recover from blips without multiplying load

items.label: Circuit breaker
items.detail: Fail fast while the dependency is down; probe to recover

items.label: Bulkhead
items.detail: Separate pools per dependency, so one slow service can't starve the rest

items.label: Fallback
items.detail: Stale cache, static default or a reduced feature

items.label: Load shedding
items.detail: Drop low-priority work first to protect the core path

example.explain: After `threshold` consecutive failures the breaker opens and returns the fallback immediately, sparing both the caller's threads and the struggling dependency. After the cooldown one probe goes through: success resets the counter, while failure re-opens the breaker at once because the counter is still at or above the threshold.

lessons.tryit: Write a one-page blameless postmortem for a real incident you have seen, or for this scenario: a config push set a cache TTL to 0, so database load rose tenfold, p99 went from 80 ms to 9 s, and the service was down for 34 minutes. Include impact (with error budget consumed for a 99.9% SLO), a timeline, contributing factors, and at least four action items, each with an owner and each a system change rather than 'be careful'.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a blameless postmortem?
options: To find out which engineer caused the outage
To understand how the system and process allowed the incident and to produce tracked changes that prevent or soften a repeat
To satisfy the SLA contract
To estimate the financial cost for the finance team
questions.explain: Blamelessness keeps people honest about what happened, which is the only way to find the real contributing factors. The output is system changes with owners. Assigning blame makes people hide information, and cost estimates or SLA reporting can be side products at most.

questions.prompt: Three components in series (99.9%, 99.9%, 99.99%), and separately two independent 99% replicas in parallel. What does this print?
questions.code:
series = 0.999 * 0.999 * 0.9999
parallel = 1 - (1 - 0.99) ** 2
print(round(series, 4), round(parallel, 4))
questions.explain: In series, availabilities multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.9999 ≈ 0.99790, so the chain is less available than its weakest link. In parallel, both replicas must fail together: 1 − 0.01² = 0.9999. The common mistake is to say a chain is as available as its weakest component (0.999).

questions.prompt: Two database replicas, each 99.9% available, are advertised as giving '99.9999% availability'. Both sit in the same rack behind one top-of-rack switch, which fails. What was wrong with the calculation?
options: Nothing; this was just bad luck

The parallel formula assumes independent failures, but a shared switch (and shared power, configuration and software) correlates them; place replicas in separate failure domains and account for common-mode failures
It should have used the series formula
Availability cannot be computed for databases
questions.explain: 1 − 0.001² is only valid if the replicas fail independently. A shared switch is a single point of failure that takes out both. Real availability is bounded by such common-mode failures, so spread replicas across racks, availability zones or regions.

questions.prompt: The recommendations service starts taking 5 s per call. Product pages call it synchronously from a pool of 200 threads, and within a minute the entire site is down, including checkout. Which set of patterns would have contained this?
options: More threads in the shared pool
A short timeout and a circuit breaker on the recommendations call, a separate bulkhead pool for it, and a fallback such as a static bestseller list
Retrying the recommendations call three times
Caching the product page HTML for 24 hours
questions.explain: A slow dependency held every shared thread (Little's law: 5 s × the request rate), so unrelated paths starved. Timeouts and a breaker bound the waiting, a bulkhead confines the damage, and a fallback keeps the page useful. More threads only delay the exhaustion; retries triple the load on the slow service; a 24-hour HTML cache breaks prices and stock levels.

terms.d: Components a request needs one after another; availabilities multiply.
Redundant copies; the system fails only if all fail.
Serving a reduced experience when a dependency fails.
An incident write-up focused on systems and contributing factors, not people.

mistakes.wrong: Adding more components makes a system more reliable.
mistakes.right: Each component in series lowers availability. Only redundancy raises it.

mistakes.wrong: A postmortem should identify who caused the outage.
mistakes.right: Blame hides information. Ask how the system allowed the mistake and fix that.

takeaways: Multiply availabilities in series; combine failures in parallel.
Decide degraded modes before the outage, with circuit breakers and bulkheads.
Write blameless postmortems with owned action items.

project.title: Three written system designs with capacity estimates
project.brief: Write three design documents of 2–4 pages each: a URL shortener, a chat system and a news feed (or substitute one with a design of your choice, such as ride-hailing dispatch). Each starts from requirements and an estimate table, and every component cites the number or requirement that justifies it. This is the stage goal in written form: a system for millions of users with every choice defended.
milestones: For each design, write functional and non-functional requirements (with explicit latency and availability SLOs) and an estimate table (average and peak QPS, storage per year with replication, bandwidth, cache memory), showing the arithmetic.
Define the API (endpoints with request and response shapes) and the data model (tables or keys, with partition keys chosen and justified by the access pattern).
Draw a high-level diagram, then write two deep dives per design (for example ID generation, fan-out strategy, hot partitions), each comparing at least two alternatives in a trade-off table.

Write a failure section covering one node dying, one availability zone lost and one dependency slowing down: the user-visible effect, the degraded mode, and the consistency model clients see in each case (using module 3's terms).

Define SLIs, SLOs and a burn-rate alert for each design; then do a 45-minute mock interview on one design with a peer (or record yourself answering 'why?' for every box) and revise the document from the feedback.
project.stretch: Prototype the riskiest component of one design (for example the feed fan-out worker or the chat sequencer), load-test it, and check that your capacity estimate was within 2×; if it was not, write down which assumption was wrong.

exam.prompt: 10M daily users make 30 requests each per day, and peak is 3× average. What is the peak QPS?
exam.explain: 3 × 10⁸ requests/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 3,472 average QPS; × 3 ≈ 10,417 at peak. The shortcut 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 10⁵ × 3 = 9,000 is within 15%, which is fine for choosing an architecture.

exam.prompt: Your URL shortener's estimates are 10,000 peak redirects/s and 3 TB of data over 5 years, with a cache hit rate above 90%. A reviewer asks why you didn't propose a 30-node Cassandra cluster. What is the strongest answer?
options: Cassandra is a bad database

With a 90%+ hit rate the database sees about 1,000 reads/s, and 3 TB fits a primary-key-indexed store on a primary with replicas or a few shards (module 2); a 30-node cluster adds operational cost without meeting any requirement better
We should use the 30-node cluster to be safe
NoSQL cannot do primary-key lookups
exam.explain: Defending a design includes defending what you left out: the numbers show modest database load and a modest data size. Calling Cassandra bad, or adding capacity 'to be safe', is not tied to any requirement, and NoSQL stores are very good at primary-key lookups.

exam.prompt: In a push-based feed, each celebrity post enqueues tens of millions of timeline inserts, and ordinary users' posts then take 10 minutes to appear in followers' feeds. What is the best fix?
options: Add more fan-out workers until the backlog clears
Exempt accounts above a follower threshold from fan-out and merge their recent posts into timelines at read time (hybrid fan-out)
Switch everyone to pure pull
Drop celebrity posts from timelines
exam.explain: Celebrity fan-out is the outlier that clogs the shared queue; skipping fan-out only for those accounts removes it at the cost of a small read-time merge. More workers chase a backlog that every celebrity post refills, and pure pull makes every user's reads expensive just to fix a few authors.

exam.prompt: A service has a 99.95% availability SLO over 30 days. A single 15-minute full outage happens. Roughly what fraction of the monthly error budget did it consume?
options: About 15%
About 35%
About 69%
More than 100%
exam.explain: The budget is 0.05% of 43,200 minutes = 21.6 minutes, and 15 ÷ 21.6 ≈ 69%. Answering 35% uses the 99.9% budget (15 ÷ 43.2); one more nine halves or tenths the budget, so check which SLO you are using.

exam.prompt: Your chat gateway design uses one OS thread per WebSocket connection, and the goal is 200,000 mostly idle connections per server. A reviewer flags it. What is the issue, and what is the module 4 fix?
options: No issue; threads are free
200,000 threads cost a lot of memory and scheduling overhead for connections that are mostly idle; use non-blocking sockets with an epoll-based event loop (or goroutines on Go's netpoller)
WebSockets cannot have that many connections on one port
Use HTTP polling instead
exam.explain: Thread-per-connection hits the C10K wall: stack memory and context switches for threads that are almost always waiting. Readiness-based I/O lets one thread per core service every connection. Port numbers limit outgoing connections, not incoming ones (each connection is a distinct 4-tuple), and polling multiplies requests.

exam.prompt: Redirects look up codes in Redis, falling back to the database on a miss. Redis has a 10-minute outage, and the redirect code treats a Redis error as a 500. What is the better design?
options: Treat the cache as optional: on a Redis error, go to the database behind a concurrency limit, and shed traffic beyond what the database can take
Keep returning 500, since the cache is required for performance
Remove the cache entirely
Retry Redis three times before returning 500
exam.explain: A cache should improve the common case, not become a hard dependency. Falling back to the database with a concurrency limit keeps as many redirects working as it can safely carry (module 4's bounded queues) instead of zero. Retrying a dead Redis only adds latency, and removing the cache permanently gives up a 10× load reduction.

exam.prompt: Two independent replicas, each 98% available, run in parallel behind a load balancer that is 99.9% available (in series). What does this print?
exam.explain: The parallel pair gives 1 − 0.0004 = 0.9996; in series with the load balancer that is 0.9996 × 0.999 ≈ 0.9986. The load balancer is now the weakest link, which is why load balancers are themselves deployed redundantly.

exam.prompt: A postmortem draft says: 'Root cause: an engineer ran the cleanup script against production instead of staging. Action item: engineers must double-check the environment.' How should it be rewritten?
options: It is fine as written

Make it blameless and systemic: the root cause is that one command could target production without any guardrail; action items such as requiring an explicit production flag and confirmation, limiting how many rows the script can delete, and separate credentials per environment, each with an owner and a due date
Name the engineer, so others learn
Remove the action items, since it was human error
exam.explain: 'Be more careful' does not survive the next tired engineer at 2 a.m.; a guardrail does. Blameless postmortems treat human error as a symptom of the system's design and fix the system. Naming the engineer makes the next incident harder to investigate, because people stop sharing what they did.
